summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 468, in a complaint filed by the respondent, alleged that the respondent was guilty of an offence under section 7 read with section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The Food Inspector found that the sample was adulterated due to insect infested pieces of Kajus to the extent of 21.9% and that the same was adulterated. The respondent filed a complaint against the respondent under section 16 read with Section 16 of Prevention of food Adulteration Act. The trial court acquitted the respondent. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that in the case of food articles for which no minimum standard or purity is prescribed, the moment it is proved that a proportion of percentage of the article not being a proportion or percentage as would be covered by the rule, de minimis non curat lex is putrid, filthy, disgusting rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or being insectinfested, it would be deemed to be unfit for human consumption and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section 2(1)(f). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The true meaning of section2(1) (f) has been brought out in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Tek Chand Bhatia, ; , and the conclusion that 'it would not be necessary in such a case to prove further that the article was unfit for consumption on account of (a) its consisting wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid or disguntur or being infested, (b) or on account thereof, (c) or On account of any other cause '. [473B C] 2. The expression 'insect infestation ' has been defined in section 2 (1) of the Act to mean "any article of food which is unfit for use as a human consumption". The expression "or otherwise unfit for such human consumption" has been used in the Act. [474C D] 3. The word 'insects ' has not been defined either in the statute or in the Rules. The definition of 'insection ' has to be read disjunctively and not disjunctively. [476D] 4. The words 'or otherwise fit for human use ' in section2 (1)(a) have to be construed disjunctively, that is, in association with what precedes it. [477F] 5. The meaning of the word 'resect infective ' has also been brought into the Act by the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. [478G] 6. The dictionary meaning of 'resects ' is to be found in the context of the definition of the term 'resulting '. The term 'inspection ' has a wide connotation. It is not necessary that the word should be read conjunctively. The more proof of the whole or any part of the articles being 'filthy, put uprid, dishusting, rotten or decomposed, or disated animal or animal or being in insect fragments or dislike, would be conclusive to bring the case within the mischief of this sub clause, and it would not, therefore, be necessary to prove any further that article was fit for consumption. [479G H] 7. The fact that the food articles were not adulterated is a relevant factor to bring home the case under the Act, and the prosecution has not established by any satisfactory evidence the requirement of section 3(1). [479A] 8. The presumption of 'unfitness ' is a rebuttable presumption. The burden of proving that the articles were unfit for food is on the prosecution. [480B] 9.

The appellant was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant was an agriculturist and that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands he had taken on lease from various parties. HELD: (i) The presumption under para 3(2) of the order cannot be drawn against him. [901 B] (ii) The appellant has successfully proved that he is an agriculturist. He was in fact carrying on agricultural operations. He produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, the presumption under paragraph 3(1) could not be drawn. [1001 C] (iii) The evidence of the witnesses on the ground that they were interested in the appellant 's business was not concocted to set up a false defence. The presumption in his case cannot be draw. [1101 D] (iv) The High court was right in holding that the presumption in the case could not he drawn. The appellant had successfully proved the fact that he was an agricultural labourer. He had produced receipts and proved by oral evidence that he had been an agriculturist, and the presumption could not therefore be drawn from proof of storage only. [1102 E] (v) The burden of proving that the lands about which the witnesses spoke orally were held by him for purposes of cultivation was on the appellant.

The defendant was a monthly tenant in respect of the premises in suit. The plaintiff sued for ejectment of the defendant on the ground that the defendant was not a monthly tenancy and that the tenancy was determined by a notice to quit. The defendant contended that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court held that the plaintiff was a tenant from month to month under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act and that he was not entitled to recover possession of the land in suit, and that by reason of the payment of rent to the Receiver in the years 1925 and 1926, he became a tenant of the suit land from month 'to month under the provisions of section 116, Transfer of property Act. The High Court held that as the defendant had no authority to receive them, the suit could not be said to be one for ejectment. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the respondent was a mere tenant from year to month and that on the expiry of the second annual lease, the defendant became a monthly tenants under section 106, Transfer Of Property Act. It was not the case of the respondent that the rent was paid by the Receiver to the receiver in the year 1926. The suit was therefore one for eviction of the tenant from the land. The respondent was not liable to be evicted from the premises. The appellant was not bound to pay rent to him. The tenancy was created by payment and acceptance of rent by the receiver. The lease was for building purposes and it was a tenancy from monthto month. The rent was payable by the lessee to the lessor. The lessee was not in possession of any land in the suit. It could not therefore be said that the tenant was a 'tenant ' within the meaning of section 106 of Transfer of Properties Act.

The appellant assessee, a private limited company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards. The Income tax Officer, after the repeal of Section 137 of the 1961 Act, issued a notice to the assessee under Section 148 of the Income tax Act, 1961, calling upon it to produce the documents in support of its claim for privilege under Section 138(1)(b) of the Act. The assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice and the order of the Commissioner. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that after the repealing of Section 138 of the 1922 Act by Act V of 1964, there was no longer any impediment left in the way of a civil court to summon the production of documents filed by an assessee during the assessment proceedings before an Income tax officer after April 1, 1964, and that the finality attached to an order of Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under section 138(i)(b), had no relationship to the power of the court to summoning the production or the disclosure of any information from the income tax authorities after April I, 1964 relating to assessment years 1965 65 onwards, and therefore, the finality attaching to an orders of the commissioner with regard thereto, was not a bar to the exercise of the jurisdiction by a court to call for the production. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finality attached under the repealed Section 137 is not confined to the cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the Section is called for by any person, other than a court of law by a judicial order. [560F] 2. The effect of introduction of Section 59 B by Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act 1960 was that it entitled a person to make an application to the Commissioner for any information relating to an assessee in respect of any assessment made either under the 1922 Income tax or under the 1961 Income tax Acts, on or after April l, 1964. [561G] 3. The consequence of introduction by Taxation laws (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1960 was to continue to remain in force by virtue of the provisions of Section 139(1) and after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed by Section 138 (1)(a) of 1961 Act. [562B] 4. The right to make a request to the Income Tax Officer for any document relating to any assessee in the assessment proceeding before an income tax officer, after April 01, 1964 was not barred by the provisions contained in Section 138. [563C] 5. The power of a court under Section 139 of the Indian Income tax is limited to the matters where the documents are filed by the assessee before the income Tax authorities after the 1st April, 1964 and the Commissioner of Income Tax has the authority to furnish or cause to be furnished the information asked for on being satisfied that it is in the public interest so to do and such an order is final and cannot be called in question in any court of Law. [564D] 6. The provisions of the repealed section 137 of 1961 are not applicable to the proceedings pending before the Incometax authorities after March 1, 1965. [565F] 7. The position that emerges from the provisions in the repealed Act is that the proceedings before the authorities under the Income ' tax Act are not barred from the production in a court on being summoned by it without the approval of the Commission of Income tax. [567G] 8. The jurisdiction of the courts to summon documents from the Income taxes authorities after May 1, 1963 is limited only to the case where the income, tax authorities, even after April, 1,1964, are immune from production in any Court of law. [568F] 9.

The appellant, a minor, was married to Seinaba and he made a gift of his properties including immovable property to Seinsaba on April 7, 1944 by a registered deed. The gift was made by a deed of gift. The appellant 's father, who was the guardian of his minor wife, was not alive and there was no legal guardian of the property. The question was whether possession could be given to the wife 's mother when the gift was from the husband to his minor daughter. Held, that the gift by the husband was complete and the gift could not be completed by delivery of the properties to the donee. The intention to make the gift is clear and manifest because it was made in the presence of the mother and the donee, and the donor could nominate a person to accept the gift on behalf of the minor. The object of the gift being to enable the minor to take possession of the subject matter of the gifts, the gift can be completed only by delivery or delivery of possession to the father. The fact that the father was alive and the mother was not in a position to accept it, would not make the transfer of the ownership of the gifted property to the donor. The mere fact that a father was living at the time of the marriage in the house of his mother in law and was probably a very sick person though not in marzulmaut, would make the gifts complete under Muhammadan law and it seems impossible to hold that by handing over the deed to his wife, the gifted was complete under Mohammedan law.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration and governance of Hindu Religious and charitable institutions and endowments in the State of Madras. Section 76(1) provides for the levy of contribution which was of the nature of a tax and not a fee. The Act does not contemplate separate rules to be made in respect of each religious institution likely to obtain the benefit of services rendered by the State for which the contribution is to be levied. The Commissioner has to determine the fee for audit of the accounts of each temple separately and prescribing the method for determining the contribution. The High Court has not investigated the question whether there was a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the Government for providing services and the amounts intended to be collected from the religious institutions for whose benefit the services are to be rendered. The question whether the Commissioner had determined the audit fee under section 76(2) of the Act was not a matter which could be determined by the Court. The Court, however, held that the Commissioner was not bound to determine whether the audit fees demanded was in truth for meeting the cost of audit of a religious institution. The order of the High Court was set aside and the case remanded to the High court for disposal according to law. The appellant contended that the High Courts had not determined the cost or the audit of accounts of the temple and proceeded to observe "It is sufficient to say that the demand made of the petitioners ' temple for the payment of a sum of Rs. 1,000/ was without determination under section 77(2). The Commissioner had not fixed the amount of audit fee as required by section 76 (2) and therefore the demand for levy of the contribution was not in truth. The contention was that the order of assessment was without jurisdiction and was beyond the legislative competence of the State Legislature. Held, that the Court had not gone into the question of the validity of section 76 of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The provisions of the impugned Act did not contemplate a separate rule to be framed in respect to each religious institutions likely to obtaining the benefit thereof. The fact that the Government had to form an estimate of the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of its accounts, did not mean that the amount demanded was not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred for auditing the accounts. The amount demanded is not precisely the amount actually incurred by it for auditing its accounts.

The appellant was convicted under section 15 of the , and sentenced to imprisonment for two years. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appeal did not lie to this court as a matter of right under section 19 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the High Court affecting the right of the party aggrieved. [515C] (2) The proceeding is initiated under section 17 by issuance of a notice. The order is not an order initiating contempt proceeding. The proceeding was initiated under Section 17 by issuing a notice and the order was not an appealable order. [511D] (3) The proceedings are initiated under s.17 by issuance or issuance of the notice. It could not be the intention of the legislature to provide for an appeal to the Supreme Court as a matters of right from each and every such order made by the High court. [615E] (4) The High Courts have no power to issue notice under section 20 of the . [516F] (5) The appeal is, therefore, dismissed as being not maintainable. [ 512G] (6) The appellant 's appeal is dismissed as not maintainable and is incompetent. [525A] (7) The matter has to be decided either finally or may be. even at an earlier stage an order is made, which does decide a contention raised by the alleged contemner asking the High Courts to drop the proceeding on the ground of its being barred under section20 of the ' Act. [506B] (8) The question whether the person proceeded against has committed contempt of the High ' Court or not is a matter which is of right to be determined either finally, or may even be. Even if the alleged contemnor in response to the notice appears before the Court and asks it to drop, the proceeding is not barred.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the , and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The appellant contended that the conviction could not be sustained under section 6(1 A) of the Act as the words "in the case of a later Act" were comprehensive enough to take in " wireless telegraphy apparatus " in section 6 (1 A). Held, that the words 'in the present case ' in section 4 of the 1952 Act were comprehensive and not exhaustive. The words " in the present Act" in section 5 of the Indian Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933, were comprehensive sufficient to take within its sweep the words used in the Act, but not the content of that Act. The language of the section did not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. The intention of the legislature in passing the said Act was to expurgate section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and the words were comprehensively enough to cover the case. The object of the amending Act was not to expel the words in the statute as it was redundant and unnecessary. The word "in" in the context of the amendment of the definition of "in this Act" was not used in a statute book but in the sense of the words. The text of an enactment, the argument proceeds, is the phraseology or the terminology used in that Act, and not the contents of that statute. The context of an Act, the context in which it is used, is not the same as the language used in it. The definition of the word "immediately" in s.4 of the said act, therefore, does not prohibit possession of wireless apparatus, and therefore, the legislature though by the Act of 1948, inserted the said section in the year 1952 as the said amendment was unnecessary and redundant.

The appellant, a son of Adwaita, was the managing Shebait of the debutter estate. The properties were sold and the appellant was put in possession of the properties. The appellant filed two applications under section 36(6) (a) (ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for the reopening of the two compromise decrees mentioned in Schedules Ka, Kha and Ga. The applications were dismissed by the Subordinate Judge. The High Court held that the appellant had not proved that the decreeholders on record were in fact benamidars for another person. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The object of restoring possession of properties sold in execution of the decree to the judgment debtor is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues, but it is to be remembered that the sale itself is not annulled, and in case of default in payment of any one of the instalments, the properties are returned to the decreeholder purchaser. [991 B] (ii)(a) The court has to order the payment of the decretal amount in such instalments as it thinks proper, and clause (e) further imposes a duty on the court to give a direction in such cases that if there is default in the payment, the property restored to the Judgment debtor under clause (c) would be put back into the possession of ' the decree holder. [ 991 B C] (b) The order for restoration of possession made by both the courts below should stand.

The appellant, a company, was the owner of certain properties. The respondent, who was the assignee of the subject matter of the suit, was a transferee of the decree. The appellant, who had been the assignee, filed a suit for specific performance of the contract. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the High Court in appeal, held that the assignment was not a transfer of the property and that the assignee was not entitled to apply for leave under Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "decree holder" must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder and that, in the present case, the assignment in writing of a decree was not transfer or an agreement to transfer the decree to the respondent company by assignment in favour of the appellant. [705 B] (ii) The word "decree" in Order XXI Rule 16 means a decree passed in the same manner and subject to the same conditions as an application for execution made by the decree holder. The words 'decree holder ' must be interpreted as meaning a decree holder, in fact, and not in a case where there was no decree in existence at the time of the assignment and this position was in effect conceded by Dixit, J. [605 C D] (iii) The expression "decreeholder" in the Order XXI of the Civil Procedure Code means a person who has been granted a decree for specific relief. The expression 'decreeholder ' in the order XXI of Rule 16 of Order XXI is not defined in the Code. The word 'decree ' in Order 21 of the C.P.C. means a judgment or decree passed by a court in a suit or proceeding. The term 'decree" is not used in the sense of a judgment, decree or order passed by the court in the suit or proceedings. [700 D E] (iv) The provisions of Order 21, rule 17(1) and (2) of the code of Civil procedure are not intended to apply to a case which is transferred before the transferee can benefit from the provisions of rule 16.

The respondent, a manufacturer of steel doors, windows, sashes and other goods, entered into a contract for "sale of windows" and to promote sales of goods manufactured by it "voluntarily offered to fit" the goods and had made no separate charge for that service. The respondent, however, did not supply the windows and the windows in a specified building, and the price of the goods supplied was not taxable. The Deputy Commissioner of Excise and Taxation in appeal held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sale of its manufactured goods, undertook to fix the windows without demanding any charge for the service, and that the price was taxable. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that from the acceptance of the tender, two contracts resulted in the sale of the window, and, therefore, the contract did not fall within the purview of the Sales Tax Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The contract was a works contract and not a contract of sale. The contract may be for work to be done for remuneration and for supply of materials used in the execution of the works for a price; it may be a contract to be for sale of a chattel as a chattels to the buyer. The contracts may be of work to he done for payment of labour and for supplying materials used for the execution thereof. The service is not rendered under a separate contract nor is the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to the execution. [508 B C] The contract is one of service and the delivery of the possession of a thing is not a sale. [506 C] In the present case, the specifications of the windows were set out in the contract. The main object of the respondent was not merely to supply the window but to "fix" the windows. The services were not rendered by the appellant under a different contract or are incidental to it. The appellant had agreed to supply "motor bus being one for sale and not of service.

The appellant was charged under section 420 read with section 511 Indian Penal Code read with Section 120B Indian Penal code read with sections 120B and 420 Indian Penal. The prosecution case was that on November 8, 1967 Shanker Lal and Raj Kumar Agarwalla were found to be a broker of foreign machinery parts. The appellant was also charged under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal C.P.C. for having committed an offence punishable under section 120B read with s.120B Indian penal Code readwith section 120 B Indian Penal Act. The trial court acquitted the appellant. The High Court, however, quashed the charges framed against the appellant and convicted him. The State appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The report lodged by Ram Avtar was lodged by the police against Shanker Lal, when the latter brought a complaint against Shankerlal and Raj Kumari Agarwalla. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he was present along with Shanker Lal when the former brought washer plates in a taxi. The whole of the report was lodged with the police. The entire report was filed with the Police. The charge sheet was lodged against the accused. The evidence of the prosecution itself was that Raj Kumar was present alongwith Shanker Lal at the time of the incident. The fact that the appellant was present at the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the complaint, would hardly warrant an inference that Raj Kumari was a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar. [279A B] 2. The first charge under section420 read with S.120 B Indian penal code readwith sections 120 B and 420 I.P., Code is framed against all the three accused. It is not necessary that the charge sheet should be submitted in the court of the Magistrate. The second charge under s.420 read alongwith section 511 I. P.C., is framed by the Magistrate against all three accused, and the third charge under sections 467, 468, 471 and 120B I.PC. is framed on the basis of the evidence of Raj Kumar. The third charge is framed under section 409 read with Ss.120 A and 420 readwith s. 120 B I. PC. The fourth charge under Section 420 read alongwith s. 511 I P. C. is also framed against Raj Kumar Aggarwalla, and Shanker Lal. The rest of the charge under S.420 I.p.C is framed. The accused were discharged. The appeal filed by the State against the acquittal of Raj Kumari Aggarwalla was allowed by the High Court on the ground that so far as Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned, no case had been made out against him. [280D E] 3. The judgment of the High court is set aside and the charge framed against him is quashed.

The petitioner, a resident of Sultanbattery area in the State of Kerala, was a resident in the state of Kerala and describing himself as a commuter of the Indian Railways. He alleged that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways, adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The petitioner alleged that no accident has taken place on account for defective bridges and has pointed out that the accident of June 6, 1981 on a river bridge in the Bihar State was attributable to this factor only. The respondents denied the assertion in the counter affidavit that no accidents have taken place in the running trains, and that the accidents of June, 1981 were attributable to the petitioner only. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The fundamental right of the citizens is to be ensured, it is undoubtedly the obligation of the Union of India and its instrumentalities to improve the established means of communication in this Country. [327C] 2. The quality of the service should improve. The standard of the services should be improved. [330D] 3. The nature of the work should be such that the people are not able to perform their duties as Judges, but they must be provided and this means that accidents have to be avoided, attack on the persons of the passengers, and prying on their property has to stop. [328E] 4. The responsibility cast by the Railway Act and the Rules under it must be complied with. It is not the duty of the State Government and its instrumentality to improve this great public utility in an effective way and with an adequate sense of urgency. [332F] 5. The obligation cast by Railways Act and Rules under them must be fulfilled. [333G] 6. The duties cast by Railway Act, and the rules under it should be complied within the time limit prescribed by the Rules. [340C] 7. The obligations cast by these Railways Act, the Rules and the Regulations under it are to be complied in a phased manner. [341D] 8. The State Government has limitations, both of resources and capacity, yet we hope that the Government and the Administration would rise to the necessity of the occasion and take it as a challenge to improve This great public interest in an efficient way and With an adequate understanding of the situation, the Government would rise in the necessity and take the same as a Challenge to improve. [342F] 9. The burden of proving that the petitioner has not been able to discharge his duties as a Judge is on the petitioner. [343G] 10. The onus of proving the existence of a public utility should be on the person who asserts the existence. [344G] 11. The duty cast by this Act and rules under the it must, therefore, be compliedwith.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. The lands were acquired by the State Government under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The appellants filed applications for restoration of the lands on the ground that they were not entitled to restoration of their lands. The applications were rejected by the Collector on the grounds that the orders passed by the Revenue Tribunal were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, and hence the applications for restoring the lands were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal. The appeals were dismissed by the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal on the view that the applications were barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the applications. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal had no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it was obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits and to record its decision even though there was default on the part of the appellant to appear in the appeal. [143 B] (2) The expression "decide it on merits" in Regulation 20 is not used in the sense of "decided ex parte" and it is obligatory on the Tribunal to decide an appeal on merit even though the default on its behalf was not due to any default on his part. [144 C] (3) The words "decides it on merit" in the context of Regulation 20 are wide enough to include in its scope and ambit an application for restoration. [145 D] (4) The word "deciding" in regulation 20 is used in a wider sense and it means "decided by the Tribunal". The word 'decide ' is used to denote the decision of the Tribunal on merits. The word has been used in contradistinction to the word "decision" and the word 'decision ' has been defined in the Act. [146 E] (5) The term "declared" in section 20 of the Jagirs Abolition Act is wide enough and it includes not only the decision on merits but also the decision or order of the Revenue Court.

The appellant 's case was that the respondent 's father had been dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy and that the village Telibandha was dedicated to him as early as 1857 by Dinanath Sao himself and later on in the year 1896 when a partition took place between his descendants who were up till 1857 when a division took place. The appellant ' case was, however, that the dedication of the village to Shri Ramchandra Swami was not proved. The trial court held that the appellant ' s case was not established and that there was no absolute dedication of village Telabandha to the deity. The High Court agreed with the Trial Court that dedication by Dinnath Sao was made in favour of the deity and that no trust was created thereby. The question for decision was whether by the Punch Faisla Award of 1896 an absolute dedication was made, in favour Of the deity or whether the village was given in full proprietorship to Ramsaran Lal. Held, that there is no absolute endowment of the Village Teli Dasi and no trust could be created thereby, and the High Court was right in holding that the plaintiff 's suit was not maintainable. The fact that there were no words in the document (the Panch Faisala Award) clearly shows an intention that the property belonged to the family with only a charge on it for the temple. The document (which was the Panch Faishla Award) also clearly shows that the intention was that Ramsara Lal would not have the absolute ownership of the property. The mere fact that the document was not a single word in Bagchi Award does not make an absolute endowment. The deed (the Panchas) clearly and unambiguously shows an agreement to the contrary. The words "from the profits and income of mouza Teli outpost" in the deed clearly show an intention to the effect that the properties belonged to 'the family with merely a charge thereon for the expenses of the temple and did not make any absolute dedication. The word "from" in this document is not defined in the Act. The expression "from profits and gains of mouzas Borsi and Teliroi" in section 2(1) of the Act means "from all profits and profits of mauzas". The word 'from ' has been defined in section 3(1)(a) of that Act to mean "from any profits and losses of mahazas, or from any profits or gains of any other kind whatsoever". The words 'from the income and profits ' in section 4(1), therefore, mean "the income and gains derived from the property of the family". The expression 'from profits ' is not used in the sense in which it is used in section 5(1). The word has been used in a sense in the context of the definition of the word 'income ' in the Income Tax Act. It is not necessary that the word should be given a restricted meaning. The term 'from " profits and loss of mahzas" in s.4(1 ) of the Income tax Act means the income derived from property of a Hindu undivided family. The definition of "income" in that section is wide enough to include income derived by a Hindu Undivided Family from property which is not the subject matter of the assessment. The income of a family is not a part of the income of the Hindu undivided Family. The property of an undivided family is a separate property and the income is not liable to be assessed to tax. The object of the section is to give a restricted interpretation to the words "in the course of the business of the assessee" and not to give any restricted meaning to the word "income".

The appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Allahabad Bar Association. The appellants were members of the said Committee. The High Court discharged the notices. The appeals filed by the appellants were dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Chairman of the Action Committee was not actively associated with the passing of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Justice and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he was guilty of contempt. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The language used by them was unfortunate. The matter becomes clear when the High court said "we do not propose to punish contemners Nos. 1 & 2 for the contumacious conduct of which we have adjudged them guilty though we express our strong. disapproval of that conduct and hope that the indiscretion will not be repeated". [602C D] 2. The words "indiscretion" in the resolution are not intended to be used in the sense of a mere desire to punish the guilty. The word "independent" is used in a very wide sense. It is not necessary to refer in detail to the same. [603D] 3. The expression "indecendent" in section 14 of the U.P. High Court 's Amalgamation Order, 1948 in a most partisan manner under the influence of Allahabad Bar. is not intended merely to be a mere wish to punish a guilty. [ 602E] 4. The use of words "in the interest of justice" in clause 14 of U. P. High Courts ' Amalgamation order, 1948, in a more partisan manner, under the control of Allahabad High Court, does not mean that the members of a Bar do not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. If lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. It was not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner. [ 604F] 6.
