The appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother, respondent No. 1 were entered into a compromise with the respondents Nos. 5, 6 and 7. The arbitrators made an application before the Sub Registrar for registration of the award. The Sub Registrar rejected the application on the ground that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take back the award for presenting the same for registration. The appellants filed an application under section 15 of the . The Sub Judge dismissed the application holding that during subsistence of interim injunction on the arbitrator to maintain Status quo the arbitrator could not taken back the Award for presenting it for registration, and that the limitation for the registration of award had already expired. The High Court ordered that the arbitrators ' application dated 14th of August, 1978 should be kept pending and be heard when the injunction order was vacated. On appeal by special leave, the appellants contended that the order made by the Sub Judge directing the arbitrators not to keep the award in the custody of the court was wrong and without jurisdiction, but no arbitrator could be compelled to disobey the order of the Court and if in compliance or obedience with court of doubtful jurisdiction, he could not have presented the award within the time as the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending, namely, 28th of January, 1978 to 24th November, 1983 should be excluded in view of the principle laid down in section 15. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order made on 28th January,1978 was the date of the order and the award was in the possession of the SubRegistrar. The award was made on 29th of November, 1982 and before the expiry of the four months from 28th November 1977, the award had been filed in the court pursuant to the order dated 24th June, 1985. [692G H] 2. The period during the pendency of the judicial proceeding was to say, from 28.1.1978 to 24.11.1983. The sub Registrar pursuant to this order of High Court on 24th of June,1985 found that the award is presented within time as it was in custody of court and there is ample evidence as it would appear from the narration of events hereinbefore made that the arbitrator had tried to obtain the custody by the court. The said order was passed on 28.11, 1983 and the Sub Registrars were directed to keep this award in their custody. [613B C] 3. The question of limitation for registration is a mixed question of fact and law. The expression "the date of commencement of the proceedings" in section 14 of the , is not defined in the Act. The word "the day of commencement" in the context of section 14 is not used in the sense of the day of the commencement of proceedings. The words "the last day of such commencement" are not defined. The term "the first day of January" is not a fixed day. The date of starting of the proceeding is not the date on which the court has to commence the proceeding. The court has no power to extend the time for filing the award beyond the period of limitation. [594C D] 4. The provisions of section 15 are not intended to be used in a technical sense. The legislature has used the expression "in the course of the progress of the suit" in its ordinary sense. It is not intended that the court should be given a liberal interpretation so as to advance the cause of justice. [599E F] 5. The language of section 16 of the Act is clear and unambiguous. The intention of the legislature is to give effect to the provisions of the statute. The object of the legislation is to provide for the speedy disposal of the suits and for matters connected therewith.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The appellant had four sub tenants, three of them also shifted to the new premises which were let to the appellant by the respondent. The respondent gave notice to the respondent to vacate the premises on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The defence of the respondent was that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises. The trial court held that the tenancy by the letter of June 7, 1948, was a new tenancy and not a continuation of the old and that the sub tenants were only licensees of the landlord and not licensees of his landlord. The High Court in appeal confirmed the order of the trial court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The respondent had waived his right in regard to the prohibition against sub tenancy and the provision in section 13(1)(e) was for the protection of his rights which he was entitled to waive. [227 D] (ii) The appellant was not entitled to the protection under section 13 (1)(a) of the Act. The question is not merely of waiver of statutory rights enacted for the benefit of an individual but whether the Court would aid the appellant in enforcing a term of the agreement which section 15 of the Bombay Act declares to be illegal. [228 E] (iii) The right of the tenant to sue for ejectment on the grounds of subletting being a personal right for his benefit, the landlord must be taken to have waived it as by an express contract he had allowed the tenant not to sub letting and consequently he could not evict the appellant under section 12(1) (e) of Act.

The respondent Board, a private limited company, was constituted under the provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. The Board was constituted by the State Government under the Act. The State Government issued a notification dated August 31, 1990, under section 3(1) of the Act, declaring the respondent Board to be the Managing Committee of the respondent Company. The respondent Board filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notification dated September 31,1990, and the notification of August 31. 1990, issued under section 4(1). The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Board that the finding reached by the Standing Committee that the fabrication was done at the behest of either the candidate or the parents or guardian was based on records, and that the decision of the Divisional Board to which they were members and the decision was on behalf Of the State Board, was based upon the evidence on record. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The finding reached in the impugned notification is based on the evidence available on record and is not supported by any evidence or if the order as passed in contravention of the statutory provisions of law or in violation of the principles of natural justice, the court has no jurisdiction to quash the order merely on the ground that different view could possibly be taken on the basis of the evidence. [798C D] 1.2 The finding recorded by the Education Standing Committee is based upon evidence on the record. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. [789E] 1:3 The conclusion reached by a Standing Committee, that the construction of the moderators ' mark sheets was done after the scrutiny by the concerned officials in the office of the State board at Bombay and before the moderators' mark sheets were taken out to Pune to feed the computer, is amply borne out from the record and it is not disputed that all the students admitted, the factum of fabrication and it was to his or her advantage and that he or her benefit and that they were parties to the fabrication and the fabrication were done at their behest. [788F G] 1 :4 The conclusion arrived at by the High court that the fabricated marks were done in the presence of the examinees and their parents or guardians is amply supported from the records. It is, therefore, clear that the conclusion reached was based solely on the admission made by the examinee or their parents and guardians.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellants were found guilty of criminal conspiracy and were convicted under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The appellants contended that the offence was not one of criminal offences but one of conspiracy and that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. Held, that the conviction of the appellants was not justified. The offence was one of a criminal conspiracy. The object of the Act was to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and that it could come into play only when there was no offer to give an d acceptance of a bribe by a public servant. The words "any person" in section 5 of the Criminal Procedure Code are wide enough to include a public servants. The definition of "public servant" in the Act is wide enough and includes a public officer. The word "public" in clause (c) of section 5 means a public official as defined in section 21 of the Penal Code. The expression "public servants" in cl. (d), means a person who is in possession, for which the accused person cannot satisfactorily account, of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income may be proved, and on such proof the Court shall presume, unless the contrary is proved, that he is guilty of the offence. The section does not say that the public servant is a public Servant. The Act does not provide for any punishment for criminal misconduct by a person in the discharge of his official duty. The provisions of the section do not make any distinction between a public and a public service. The offences under section 4(1) are not offences under the Act. The charge under section 6(1)(d) is not one under section 7(1). The offence under section 8(1), therefore, is not a criminal offence.

The appellant Bank, a bank, was the guarantor of the respondent Bank. The respondent Bank, in the suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368.04 P. from the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor, filed a suit for the recovery of the amount due from the appellant Bank. In the suit, the appellant bank claimed that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal debtor pledging oil tins and that the respondent bank was not discharged from his liability under the guarantee. The trial Court found that there was negligence on the part of the Bank with regard to the safe custody of the pledged oil tin and that as the contract of guarantee entered into by the surety with the Bank was independent of the pledge of goods given by the principal creditor, the surety was discharged to the extent of the value of security and that in view of the combined operation of sections 139 and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, the respondent was discharged from the liability under guarantee. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the Bank had failed to exercise such care as a prudent man would in the circumstances of the case which resulted in the loss of security, namely, pledged oil and, therefore, in view Of combined operation, sections 139 & 141 of Indian Contract act, the sureties were discharged to that extent. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The surety was entitled to restitution. [922D] 2. The High Court was right in holding that the creditor having lost one security, the bond was discharged. [822F] 3. The appellant Bank was not discharging the obligation undertaken under the letter of guarantee. It was difficult to entertain a contention that section 141 would not be attracted and the surety would not he discharged from its obligation undertaken by the bank. [883C] 4. The guarantor was entitled, therefore to restitution, and the suit against the surety is decreed. [893D] 5. The bond executed by the appellant was an inescapable conclusion that the principal debt was lost on account of the negligence of the creditor Bank. [903E] 6. The guarantee of the surety in good faith contracted to offer personal guarantee on the clear understanding that the Principal debtor had offered security by way of pledge of the goods and the goods were to be in the custody of creditor Bank, yet the surety could not be discharged from obligation undertaken thereunder. [864F] 7. The liability of the guarantor is discharged to a extent of his security lost as provided by section 141. [874G] 8. The principal debtor was entitled under the terms of the guarantee to the benefit of every security which the creditor has against the principal borrower at the time when the contract was entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the surety knew of such other security offered by the Principal creditor, if the creditor loses or without the consent of the principal. [854A] 9. The sureties were not discharged in the event of the default of the sureties. The Bank was entitled only to restitution and the decree against the guarantor was set aside.

The appellant was the son of Amritrao patel, who was the holder of a "patelki inam" lands. The appellant was a member of the family of Amrit Rao. The respondent No. 1 was the owner of the "p Patelki inam " lands. He was the proprietor of the said "patels and Patwaris" lands and the appellant was entitled to his share in the "Patelki Inam" lands as a member thereof. The Government of Bombay, by a notification dated August 28, 1922, declared that the " patelki inams" lands were divided and the lands in suit were allotted to the share of the appellant. The respondents filed a suit for a declaration that the appellant 's rights in the lands were not affected by the resumption proceedings relating to the jagir on the footing that they were separate from and independent of the jagir. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the lands belonged to the appellant and the grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government and that the grant made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag was recognised by the Government as a "service inam" by the Indian Government. The appeal to this Court was filed on a certificate granted by the High Court. Held, that the rights which the appellant had in these lands were rights of dealing with the property as owners, subject to a member 's family, irrespective of whether he performs the service or not. The grant was not a service grant and no question of title arose against Government, even though the lands are shown as excluded from the jagir of Nawabag. The mere fact that the land was given by way of emoluments for the patel 's office, no question could arise of the grant of a share in emoluments. The right to a share was not an absolute right and no right was given to a person to claim a share. The rights which a member had in the past were not subject to any right to resume the same. The fact that a member was entitled as of right to the " Patelki" lands was not conclusive. The question whether a member is entitled as a right to an interest in the emoluments of the patels or the holder thereof was not one of fact. The claim of a member for a share of his emoluments was not based on any right or title. The order of Government dated August 27, 1922 did not confer any new right nor did it deprive anyone of any subsisting right in respect of the 'patel ' lands.

The appellant, a Cutchi Memon, was a Cutch Memon. He was born in the year 1928. He died in 1945. The appellant 's father, who was the son of the deceased, was the sole surviving son of his father. The respondent, who had settled down in Madras, was born to him in 1945 and he was born on January 1, 1946. The respondents, who were the sons of the appellant, filed a suit for partition of the properties in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Madras, and for a declaration that the appellant was entitled to the properties as his son. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, in appeal, held that the rules of Hindu law applicable to Cutchi memons governed matters of succession and inheritance only. The question as to which personal law, sects among the Muslims, such as the Khojas and the Memons, would be subject to in matters of property, succession and succession, including rules as to joint family property, the right of a son in it by birth and the devolution thereof by survivorship, was not disputed. The appeal to this Court was filed by the appellant on the ground that the rule of Hindu Law applicable to cutchi Memons governed the matter of succession, and that the High Court was wrong in holding that the respondents were governed by the Hindu Law as to stridhan. HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in holding the rule applicable to the Cutchi Coron, and the High Courts had rightly held that in the absence of a special custom as to succession, the Hindu law of inheritance would apply to the cutchi memon. [233 B] (ii) The question whether the respondents are governed by Hindu Law or not, was one of fact. The rule of law applicable in the case of a family trading concern is that the property of a person who has been made insolvents, is governed by a Mahomedan law. The law of succession is governed in matters relating to succession and devolution by the rules as well as the rules. [234 C] (iii) The rule applicable in a case of succession to a property held by a person in his own right, is not a rule of succession. The rules of succession are not applicable to a case where the person who had been made a insolvent has already acquired a right by birth in the property held in his favour by his father, a right expressly saved by section 3 of the Act. [235 D] (iv) The law applicable is the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and not the Hindu Laws. [236 E] (v) The rules relating to the succession and the succession of a deceased person are governed in the matter Of succession and as such, the rule is applicable to all cases of succession or inheritance. [237 G] (vi) The provisions of section 3 are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Hindu laws.

The appellants are manufacturers of fabrics. They manufacture fabrics of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage. It has been held that the yarn which is produced at an intermediary stage in the mill of the appellants and subjected to the integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics, will be liable to payment of excise duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 of the Rules. The appellants are liable to pay excise duty on the yarn after it is sized for the purpose of weaving it into fabrics. The respondents are also liable to excise duty under the Central Excise Act, 1944. The High Court, however, held that since the yarn was produced at a intermediate stage in an integrated process, it will be a case of removal for the purposes of payment of duty. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the retrospective effect given by section S I will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The language of rule 9(1) admits of only one interpretation and that is that the specification that has to be made by the Collector is of any premises appurtenant to the place of manufacture or production of the excisable goods. [707C] 2. The specification is not required to be given and, in the instant case, the appellants are not liable to duty. [807D] 3. The expression "place of removal" has been given retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force. The definition of "place" in section 2(1)(a) of the Finance Act, 1982, is not applicable to the facts of the instant cases. [700E] 4. The word "place", in the definition of the word "premises" in the Finance Acts, 1982 and the Explanation to rule 9, does not contain any definition of 'place of manufacture '. The description of the goods in the explanation to rule9(1), therefore, cannot be made of the place where the goods are produced, cured or manufactured. [607F] 5. The words "place or premises appurtenant thereto" in rule 9 (1) admit of only two interpretation and, therefore, the expression "premises appurtenant thereto". The specification that have to be make by the collector is of no consequence. [ 700G] 6. The Explanation to Rule 9(2) does not refer to the goods which are produced at the intermediate stage of an integrated manufacture of another commodity by deeming such production or manufacture of the commodity at an earlier stage to be removal from such place or premises of manufacture. [750A] 7. The explanation to Rule9(2), however, does indicate that the description that has been made by Collector is only when the goods were removed from the factory premises it will not be a "place where the excisable article is manufactured or cured or if such excisable goods are used in the manufacture of any other commodity in the same place, this cannot be done without payment of Excise duty at the place and in the manner prescribed. [751B] 8. The use of the expression 'place ' in the Explanation does not mean that the goods produced or manufactured in any place or factory at an end of the manufacture or manufacture would be removed from such premises or premises immediately before such consumption or utilization. [753C] 9. The meaning of the words "premises belonging to the manufacturer" in Rule 9 is that if a commodity is taken outside the factory it will become removal from the place or the premises immediately after such consumption, or utilization, and the goods manufactured within the factory are removed from one plant to another it will also be a 'place where such goods are manufactured or produced. [754D] 10.

The petitioner filed a suit for a declaration that the scheme published under section 68 C of the Act was illegal, void and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the respondents from proceeding with the hearing of the suit till the disposal of a special leave petition before this Court. The trial court dismissed the suit. The petitioner filed an application before the Civil Judge for staying the hearing and approving the scheme. The Civil Judge dismissed the application. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the State Government (the Hearing Authority under section68 D of the , is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil court to issue an order of injunction restraining a Hearing Authority from proceeding further with the proceedings. [545C] 2. The procedure laid down for the preparation of the scheme is contained in sections 68 C and 68 D of Act. The rules also provide for the particulars to be incorporated in the scheme and the other provisions contained in Chapter IVA of the . [546D] 3. The Rules also provide that on the publication of the Scheme under section 69 C of Act, any person who is aggrieved by the proposed introduction of the schemes is entitled to file his representations and objections and to appear before the Hearing Authority. The rule also provides for the details to be included in the Scheme published under Section 68 C. [544E] 4. The scheme has been duly published under s 68 C, and it becomes final. [546F] 5. The provisions of Chapter IV A of the are mandatory and are not mandatory. The State Government is entitled under section 70 D of that Act to file its objections and representations and to pass appropriate orders thereon. [547G] 6. The power of the Hearing authority under section 67 D of , is absolute in character, and is not subject to any limitation. [548F] 7. The powers of the hearing authority under Section 69 D of . are exclusive in nature and it cannot be said that the hearing Authority under Section68 D is exclusive. The proceedings before the hearing authorities under section 66 D of ' the Act are exclusive. [549G] 8. The Court is not entitled to issue any order of temporary injunction restraining an Hearing Authority or the Hearing Authorities from proceeding in the suit and exercising its statutory functions. [550H] 9. The civil court is directed to dispose of the suits in the light of the observa tions made in this order.

The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellant had obtained a bribe from the appellant and that the money was paid to him in repayment of the loan by him to Russel Nathaniel. The appellant was convicted under section 161, Indian Penal Code and section 161 of the Indian Penal code. The High Court set aside the order of sanction and convicted the appellant under section 6(2). The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : The order of the sanction in the present case satisfies the requirements of section 6 of the Act. The order was not excessive. [184 D] The order passed by the Judicial Committee has no application to the present appeal. [185 E] The appellant had been guilty of grossly abusing his position as a police officer and extorted money from Russel, Nathannyiel and his wife and also a gold ring from Roshan Lal. The charge under section 4(2)(d) of Prevention of corruption Act is established. [186 D] In the present ease the appellant was guilty of gross abuse of his position on the part or the appellant. The conviction of the appellant for the offence under section 3(2), read with section 5 (1)(d), of the prevention of Corruption act, 1947, was not justified. [187 E] In view of the fact that the offence charged and the charge under that section is established, the conviction of appellant under that Section is not excessive and the sentence imposed is not unreasonable.

The appellant was convicted by the Special Judge under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The sanction accorded by the appellant was not a valid sanction. The sanction was not valid. The appellant had not applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the sanction accorded was not in a valid one. [1005 C] (ii) The sanctioning authority had not given any reason for the grant of the certificate. The order granting the certificate was not invalid. The sanctioning authorities had not considered the relevant papers and the evidence of the witnesses. The documents which were placed before the appellant were relevant to the only question before him whether he should or should not accord his sanction to the prosecution of the appellant. [1015 D] (iii) The order of the Special judge was not an invalid one. The Special judge had not taken into consideration the relevant documents and the materials placed before him. The papers which were produced before him were relevant for the purpose of the prosecution. [105 E] (iv) The Special Judge had not properly considered the evidence and the circumstances of this case. The special judge had applied his minds to the fact and circumstances in the case. He had applied its mind to all the relevant materials and had applied the mind to those facts and the circumstance of the present case. [115 G] (v) The appellant was entitled to the benefit of the sanction.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground of demolition and reconstruction. The respondents contended that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and for reconstruction. They also contended that they had only a life interest in the premises in question and that it was inherent in such a life estate that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14(1)(b) as grounds for eviction were not bona fide. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction was not bona fides. The High Court in revision held that the landlord had no right to ask for eviction on the grounds of demolition, reconstruction and reconstruction, and that the tenant had only an life interest and right to enjoy the property for his life. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that there was no possibility or any objection from the daughters of the settlor or from any other remainder man. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression landlord is defined under section 2(6) as follows: " 'Landlord ' includes the person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a building whether on his own ac count or on behalf or on account of another or on his behalf and others or as an agent, trustee, executor, administrator, receiver or guardian or who would so receive the rents or be entitled to receiving the rent, if the building were let to a tenant". [275E] 2. The word landlord is used in the context of the Act. The Act with which we are concerned is a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act (See M/s Raval and Co. vs K. Thus a controversy that may arise between a landlord and others, who are not his tenants under the Act, is outside the ken of this Act. [275F] 3. The definition of landlord is wide enough to include the person whose interest is in the property and who admittedly has been on his personal right under the Deed of Settlement as a trustee receiving rents of the premises from the tenants. [276G] 4. The term landlord is not defined in section 2 (6) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The words "landlord" are defined in Section 2(7) as meaning "any person who has been receiving or was entitled to received the rent or be deemed to receive it". [276F] 5. The landlord is a person who holds a life interests in the building and who has not been on the own right under this Deed of settlement as a Trustee receiving rents from the tenant. [277G] 6. The provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 are not applicable to the facts of the case. [278F] 7. The Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to decide the question as to whether the landlord was entitled for eviction under section 14 (1) (b) of Act. It was not open to the landlord in the present case to contend that there is no possibility of any objection to the daughters or from the daughter of the executant or from some other remainder person. [279G] 8. The question as has been sought to be established in the case by proving that there are no possibility and any objection was from the sisters of the testatrix or from anyone other remainderman. [280F] 9. The tenant has only a right to get the rent for his own life. The right to evict the tenants is not a right which can be taken away by the provisions of section 14 of the Rent Act. In this case, the landlord has only an interest in a premises and who had been on her own right.

The respondent decree holder, a tenant of a grove, was granted a lease of the grove to the appellant. The lease was for a period of five years. The respondent decreeholder filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that the trees were not part of a ' grove '. The appellant 's case was that the land was not part and parcel of a "land" and that the respondent decree was not binding on him. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the appellant was entitled to the protection of section 6(a) (i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that the respondents were not entitled to protection of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The definition of the intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of U. P. Zamindari and Land Reform Act, 1951, is wide enough to include trees, which are parts of groves, and grove land. [782B] (2) The word "intermediary" in section 18(1)(a) of that Act means "inter intermediary" and an inseparable part is always included in the whole. [882C] (3) The expression "intermediate" in the definition of intermediary ' in section 3 (13) means "any person who is in possession or in possession of any land or other property". The word 'intermediaries ' in the Act means a person who has been in possession and enjoyment of any such land or property. [877D] (4) The term "interlocutory" in Section 18(2) means a right to be heard and determined by the Court. [878E] (5) The words "interval" in sub section (1)(b) of section 18 are wide enough, to include all trees, including grove land, and groves and grove lands. [879F] (6) The High Courts were wrong in not holding that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6 of the Land Reforms and Land reforms Act, 1952, the right in trees of grove land was the right of the intermediaries.

The appellants were charged with an offence under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The trial court convicted the appellants under Section 326 IPC and awarded them rigorous imprisonment of two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ each. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The conviction of the first appellant for an offence punishable under Section 304 Part I IPC is not permissible. The conviction and sentences of all the appellants for the offence under section 302 IPC are maintained but without the aid of Section 149 IPC. [89B] 1.2 The conviction for an offences under Section 324 IPC is set aside and the appellants are convicted for an offense under Section 325 IPC. The appellants are sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment each for a period of three years and pay a sum of Rs, 1,500/ each to the first accused. The sentence of imprisonment for one year and to fine of rupees one thousand each is maintained but with the aid Of Section 149, IPC. In view of the sentences recorded for offence under Sections 302 and 324 IPC, the appellants 2 and 3 are sentenced for an additional period of two months and to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months. [90F G] 1:3 The conviction under Section 307 IPC is maintained and the sentence of fine of Rupees one thousand is maintained. [91F] 1 :4. The offence under Sec. 325 IPC is punishable with imprisonment for two years each. [92F] 2.1 In the instant case, the injuries on the deceased had been caused by all the four appellants and that the death of Suku had occurred due to the injuries inflicted by them. The injuries on his person had been inflicted by all of them and that he had not been charged for the substantive offence of murder under Section 323 IPC. Therefore, the conviction of all of the accused for an act under Section 148 IPC is upheld. [93G H] 2:2. The prosecution case is that the appellants were armed with deadly weapons and were armed by the first appellants with a chopper and the injuries caused by them were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death of the deceased. The medical evidence shows that the injuries were caused by blunt weapons. The injury on the person of the injured had been sustained by the deceased and the medical evidence also shows that it was not possible to say that the injury inflicted by the appellants was either individually or taken collectively with the other injuries caused to the deceased, sufficient in their ordinary course to cause his death. [94G H; 95A] 2 :3. The intention to cause the death is not an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 and cannot, therefore, form the basis for conviction for the offences under Sections 304 Part 1, IPC without a specific charge having been framed against him as envisaged by law. [95B] 2(a) The intention of causing death of a person is not a mere desire to cause bodily injury. It is not necessary that the intention to inflict the injury must be such as to cause an injury which is sufficient in ordinary course or nature to causes death. The knowledge of the injury is sufficient to cause it. [96C] 2.(b) The knowledge that the person who caused the injury has been likely to cause such bodily injury as is sufficient, in the normal course of things to cause that death, is sufficient. [97D] 2 (c) The fact that the accused had caused the injuries with a weapon which was sufficient in his ordinary course would not make him guilty of an offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. [98F] 3.

The assessee, a non resident assessee, was assessed to income tax on cash basis for the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69. The assessee claimed that it was not following any particular method of accounting regularly in the past years, that it had not actually received any income in all these four years, and that it did not actually receive any income from the said amounts in its books at Coventry. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash receipt basis for 1967 68, and the assessee was not entitled to any deduction under section 5(2)(a) of the Income Tax Act. The Tribunal, however, held that since the Indian Company had credited to the assessee in its accounts for the relevant years, no tax was payable by it. The High Court, on reference, held against the assessee. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the assessee could be said to have received the royalty amount only when it receives the same in U.K. in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own books at coventry, and since it did rot actually receive the amount, it did so in U K. Section 145 was relied upon by the assessee to say that the method of accountancy regularly adopted by an assessee is binding upon the department; on that basis it was argued that if the assessee is proved to have maintained its accounts with respect to royalty amount on cash receipts basis, then there is no receipt until it is received by it in UK. In this connection, it may be noticed that in its returns relating to the assessment year 1967 68 the assessee stated that it is maintaining its accounts on cash payment basis and since the assessee did not receive the amounts, it could not have been said that the amount was not actually receipt of income by the assesee. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The method of account adopted by the assesses for the accounting years is really irrelevant. [105B] 1.2 The method adopted by it for all its income was really irrelevant and that section 5 (2)(b) governs it irrespective of the fact whether it maintains its accounts in U .K. or in U,K. [106C] 1:3. The method followed by the Income tax Officer for the purpose of accounting in regard to royalty and that the said method of accounts adopted by him for all the years is obviously irrelevant. In these circumstances, it must be held that in the circumstances of the case, the method adopted was really relevant. [107D] 1 :4. The question whether there is any conflict or inconsistency between section 5 and section 145 of the Act or whether the assessee has received the amount. [108E] 1.(a) The assessee could not be said that it has received any amount. The mere entry in the account books of the Indian company does not amount to receipt of Income by the appellant. [109E] (b) The fact that the Indian Companies had credited the said amount to the account of the appellant in its Books of the India Company does not mean that the money was not really received. [110F] (c) The mere fact that it maintained its books on cash payments basis does not lead to the conclusion that the payment was not made. [111F] 1(a) In the instant case, it is not necessary to express any opinion on the question whether the amount is actually received, but the assessee firm was a debtor in respect of that amount and unless the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt, clause (a) cannot apply.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The evidence of the approver was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of the first accused upon which the High Court had no jurisdiction to convict upon his testimony alone. [834 B] (ii) The statement of the appellant was not corroborated in material particulars and qua each accused. The evidence was sufficiently corroboration of the accomplice 's story. [ 834 C] (iii) The conviction of an accused on the testimony of an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal, the courts nevertheless cannot lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice which in the words of Martin B in Res. vs Boyes (1) as follows : "The evidence of an approver is admissible in law (R. v Attwood; , , , referred to. (iv) The rule of caution is that the court should be slow to depart from the rule Of prudence and Practice which in its words of Lord Reading C. J. in R. vs Baskerville (1), as follows: "The rule of practice is almost always unsafe to convict on his testimony only, but the judge should point out to the jury that it is within their legal province to convict him upon such evidence, but, the judge must point out, to the verdict of the jury, that it was within their jurisdiction to acquit upon such unconfirmed evidence. The rule is not a rule of law but a rule which is a rule in practice, and it is almost invariably unsafe to conviction upon his evidence alone. The courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence of such a witness without corroboration in material details. [820 E F] (v) The principle of prudence is that there should be corroboration of an injured witness in material facts and circumstances. The court will, however, be slow in departing from the rules of prudence, based on long experience, which requires some independent evidence implicating the particular accused.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that on July 8, 1961 a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.W. Chaudhury did not challenge the findings of the High Court on questions of fact but the appellant was convicted under section 161 Indian Penal Code. The High Court held that the appellant could not be convicted of the charges because he was not a "public servant" within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal code. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21, cl. (12) of section 2 of the Act. [695 B] (ii) The words "public servants" include "every officer in a service or paid of a local authority or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of any other law that he could be said to be a public servant within the definition of section 3 of the , and also of section 5 of the prevention of Corruption. [795 C] (iii) The word "public" in section 2(12) includes "every person in the employment or pay or of the Government". The words 'public servant ' include every officer in any service or payment of a public duty. [700 D] (iv) The expression "public Servant" in the definition is not defined in the Act but in the context of the definition it is used in the sense of a person who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty and is therefore a public officer within the ambit of section21(9) of that Act. The words are not defined either in the Code or in the Indian Evidence Act. They are not intended to be used in any other sense. [750 E F] (v) The definition of "public service" in s.2(12), Indian Penal, Code, is wide enough to include every person who was a public servants within the scope of the section. [751 G] (vi) The term "public officer" in cl. 12 of section 1 of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958, is not used in a sense of the term "Public servant" in that section. The word 'public ' in section 3(12)(a) of this Act is used to denote a person in a public service or a public office. The expression 'public servants ' in the section means a person appointed to any office for performance of any public duty, and includes every officer who is employed to any such office for performing any public duties.

The appellant was convicted for contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 1,000. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant in respect of contravention of Cl. 3. The appellant contended that the order regarding forfeiture of the juar seized from the house of the appellant was illegal and void as it was not passed in accordance with the provisions of the Defence of India Rules. The contention was that the High Court had set aside his conviction and sentences in respect Of contravention of cls. 3 and 4 of the Order. The State contended that r. 141(2) was ultra vires because it laid down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. Held, that r, 141(1) is within the powers conferred by section 3(1 ) of the Act and the Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. The Rules must be necessarily provide that the provisions Of the Act or any rule made thereunder or any order made under any such rule shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act. The rules must necessarily provided for the issue of a notification under the rules and they should also provide proof in the judicial proceedings. The rule must necessarily be provided for proof of judicial proceedings in the fact o.f the fact that the rule is contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the defence of India Act provides that "the provisions of this Act or of any rule or order made thereunder shall have affect notwithstanding anything contained in the Act". The Rules cannot be said to be ultra vires.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted the appellant under section 304, read with s. 34, of the Code. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High court was right in holding that the appellant was guilty of murder under section 307 read with sections 149 and 147 of the Penal Code. [682 B] (ii) The conviction of the appellant for having committed the murder of the deceased in furtherance of their common intention was bad in law. [683 E] (iii) The appellant was acquitted by the High Court on the ground that the evidence was not acceptable or by giving benefit of doubt to them. [684 C] (iv) The judgment of the High court cannot stand. [685 G] (v) The fact that the charge as well as the evidence were directed against the 4 named accused, did not necessarily mean that they did not take part in the offence. The petitioner, a manufacturer of iron and steel products, was granted a licence for import of iron & steel products. The licence holder transferred the same in favour of M/s Metalic metal Indus tries. The petitioner filed an application under Article 32 of the Constitution on 16th April, 1988 for the grant of a licence to import iron and Steel products. On 11th May, 1983, the licensing authority issued import licence No. 2959845 for Rs.20, 12,729 in favour M/S Metalic Metal Indus try. The licensing authority granted import licence to M/ s Metalic steel Indus tried. The goods were cleared on payment of duty. The respondents filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal. The revision petition filed by the petitioner was also dismissed. The writ petition filed in this Court was also rejected. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner as such has no fundamental fight to clear the goods imported except in due process of law. [626C] 1.2 The petitioner has no right to seek recourse to Article 32. [625E] 1:3. The relief under Article 226 of the Consti tution is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case. [ 625F] 1 :4. The petition is not maintainable. [650F] 2.1 In a matter of this nature where liability of a citizen to pay a particular duty depends on interpretation of law and determination of facts and the provision of a particular statute for which elaborate procedure is pre scribed, it cannot conceivably be contended that enforcing of those provisions of the Act would breach fundamental right which entitle a citizen seeking recourse to article 32 of t he Constitution. [600G] 2:2. The remedy under Article32 of the Constitu tion is wholly inapplicable. [700H] 2 :3. In a case of this kind where liability is of a person to pay the particular duty depend on interpretation or determination of questions of law as well as ques tion of fact without taking any resort to the provisions of t his Act, it is not permissible to move this Court on the theoretical basis that there is breach of fundamental right. [726G] 3.1. The question of enforcement of a fundamental right arises in this case and the writ peti tion is not entertainable. [750H] 3:2 In a given case, the petitioner has a fundamental fight against the enforcement of which alone Article 32 is attracted. [751A] 3 :3 The petitioner is not entitled to seek resort to Article 226. [753B] 4.2. In the instant case, there is no question of the enforcement o f a fundamental rights.

The appellant was the owner of a bungalow. The bungalow was sold in execution of the payment order and the properties were sold in payment of a debt binding on the family and therefore the sale in execution was not binding on him. The appellant contended that the sale was not for the illegal and immoral acts on the part of the respondent and that the property was sold for the unlawful and immoral act on the ground that the respondent had no interest left. Held, that the liability of the sons to discharge the debts of the father which were not tainted with immorality or illegality was based on the pious obligation of the son which continues to exist in the lifetime and after the death of the mother and which does not come to an end as a result of partition of the joint family property. The liability of a father, who is a managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration, incurred as a consequence of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avyavaharika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals". The liability to discharge debts of a deceased father is not a debt as such but a debt which is not tainted by immority or illegality is based on a pious obligation. The obligation of a son to discharge his debts of his father is a question of fact in each case dependent upon what was the estate put up for sale, what the Court intended to sell and what the purchaser intended to buy and did buy and what he paid for. The right, title and interest of the defaulter in one case and " of the judgment debtor" in the other. The debt of the deceased father which is a joint family debt is not the same as the debt of a joint Hindu family. The property of the husband is not his personal property but his personal properties. The father is the managing director of the family. He is the manager of the estate and he is the trustee of the property. He has no interest in the property and the property is not liable to be sold for any illegal and unlawful acts on his part. The estate of the minor son is not joint family properties.

The petitioners, who were seven in number, challenged the constitutional validity of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, and the notification issued under section 8 of the Act, as amended by the Rajasthan Goods and Goods Tax Rules, 1959. The petitioners contended that the Act was unconstitutional and ultra vires the provisions of the Constitution and that the tax was without authority of law. Held, that the proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 of the , is extra territorial in nature, because it makes the tax payable on fares and freights attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory, even though the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan. The tax is still on passengers and goods, though what it is to be determined by the amount of fare or freight. The Act and the Rules must be read harmoniously and reading them so, it is plain that the apparent mandatory language of the Rules and the Notification still retains the permissive character of the section, but only lays down what the amount is, if lump sum payment is made in lieu of payment of the tax calculated on actual fares andreights. The words "in respect of all passengers carried and goods transported by motor vehicles" and "in case of such vehicles not registered in Rajasthan to the incharge of the check post or barrier at the time of their entry into the State of Rajasthan or to the officer of the Excise and Taxation Department nearest to the point of entry into that State and having jurisdiction over that area, are not available to the State Legislature. The proviso to section 3 is extra ordinary in nature and does not affect the power of the State legislature to levy tax on passengers or goods. The word "tax" in the proviso is wide enough to include taxes on passengers, goods and goods. It is the cost of construction and maintenance which makes the difference in the tax, and no case of discrimination can be said to be made out. The expression "tax on fares" in section 3, in terms, speaks of the charge of the taxes "in relation to all passengers carrying and goods carried by motor vehicle". The tax, however, is still a tax on passenger and goods and the argument that it is not so, is not sound. The distinction between the tax on fares or freights and the tax is that the amount which is to he collected is the tax which is payable on passengers. The difference in tax is not admissible because tax on freights is a Union subject, and is not available. The fact that the rate of tax is fixed by the State Government does not mean that the State has no power to levy the tax. The State Legislature has the power to impose tax on goods and passengers. It has the right to impose taxes on goods or passengers. But the tax has to be levied on passengers as well as goods. If the tax imposed is a tax, the tax must be levied in accordance with the provisions contained in the Act. The levy of tax on the fares and the freights, therefore, is without authority. The contention that the levy of the lump sum is not a tax under the Entry, and thus, the taxes are without authority, is also not sound, because the tax itself is a State subject, but is not an "tax". The word 'tax ' in the Proviso to section 2(3) is wide and covers all taxes on fares, freights or freight, and it does not cease to be a tax.

The only limited question is whether the Labour court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back Wages. [569G] 4. The High Court has rightly directed the reinstatement of all the workmen. [570F] 5. The accused was charged with murder of his wife Churi. The prosecution case was that the accused was married to Churi deceased near about 1958. At the time of the occurrence, the accused had come to the house of the deceased and told him that he was with Churi in the house during the day but at 6 p.m. he left for Kotkhai leaving his wife alone at the house. The accused stated that he had cordial relations with his wife for the fast 14 years. The deceased was married in the village of the accused. The relations of the husband and the wife were strained. The father of the boy and the deceased were strained and the accused made the following statement: "I had cordial relation with my wife for a fast 14 year. I had cordial relationship with my husband for the last 14 years and I had no cordial relations. I was not in a position to give any satisfactory explanation for the murder of Churi." The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not sufficient to prove the guilt of the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The evidence of PW 10 was not reliable. The evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of the victim was recovered after the accused came to the residence of the father of Chururi. [11 D] (2) The statement of the witness that he saw the accused going to see film show at Kotkhali was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The statement was recorded by the Magistrate and was signed by the accused and was attested by the witnesses. The witness was not cross examined by the prosecution. The fact that the relations of Chura deceased were cordial would not, in the absence of any cogent explanation by him, point to his guilt. [12 E F] (3) The fact of the recovery of the dead bodies from the house and the fact that there was nothing to show that the police was aware of the murder was not a circumstance which could be accepted. [13 E] (4) The prosecution had failed to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that it was the accused who was responsible for the death of Chri. The plea of the defence that he did not know the murder and that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with him without the child, was not accepted. The defence had failed in proving the guilt. The trial court had rightly convicted the accused under section 302 Indian Penal Code. [14 E F; 15 A] (5) The High court was right in holding that the prosecution had proved beyond any doubt that there were no circumstances which could justify the conviction of the respondents.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the prosecution had failed to prove the complicity of Sadanand in the murder of the Collector. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. [413D] 2. The statement of a witness is not admissible against other accused persons. It is a fact that a set of witnesses who, according to the prosecution, were present when the deceased was taken into custody following the incident, have not spoken about any confession. It may be that the witness may not have supported the version that he met her husband P.W.4 on that day. The prosecution has further led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadananda at the jail, enforcement of rules became slack and there was a regular flow of food from outside. This type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav, being a follower, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. [414E F] 3. The evidence of the prosecution witnesses is not sufficient to establish conspiracy. The circumstances relied upon by the prosecution are not such as to establish the complicity or conspiracy. It has to be established and the chain has to been completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [412F G] 4. The conviction of the appellant is not sustainable. [416B] 5. The appellant was convicted under Section 302 readwith section 120B of the I.P.C. and sentenced for death.

The appellants were working as clerical and subordinate staff in the respondent company. The company was a subsidiary of the respondent Company. The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1948. The Company was a private limited company. It was a controlled company. Its main object was to provide for the establishment of a new company. In the year 1949, the company was formed and it was registered under the Companies Act, 1956. The appellant company was also incorporated in 1948. In 1950, the respondent was incorporated as a private company. On the basis of the recommendations of the Industrial Tribunal, the appellant company made a reference to the Industrial Court, Bombay, for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the company had been paying the minimum wages and dearness allowance and that the Tribunal had not considered the total effect of the increase in the basic wage and dearness allowances. The High Court, however, held that there was no justification for the Tribunal to have taken into account the comparable concerns in the same industry and provided for the same scales of dearness allowance. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which was the basis for fixing wages and Dearness allowance. The tribunal had not specifically considered what the total wage packet would be on the basis that the total wages packet including basic wages and other dearness allowance were higher than the highest in the comparable concern. [375 E] (ii) The Industrial Tribunal had ignored the fact that the appellant was a company in the region and in fixing the same scale of dearness allowances for factory workmen as in the case of clerical staff. The Industrial Court had not given any finding on the question whether the total pay packet in the appellant 's concerns could bear comparison with the total salary packet of comparable concerns. [376 G] (iii) The tribunal has not specifically dealt with the matter in which it had made comparison for clerical and other staff. It has also not considered what would be the total amount of dearness Allowance fixed by it as well as dearness allowance fixed by the Tribunal.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa, filed a suit against the respondents for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof free from encumbrances and for other ancillary reliefs. The trial Court held that the Rajinama had not the effect of transferring the interest of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property to the mortgagees and that the appellants were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking accounts the mortgages had redeemed themselves. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal in part with the result that the suit was dismissed so far as the claims of the appellants to the extent of the share in the mortgage property were concerned. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Rajinma 's share was a complete relinquishment of his interest, but as regards Annappa 's half share in it, he agreed with the District Judge 's conclusion that Shiddppa was the manager and karta of the joint family and that in the matter of passing the Raj inama he had acted in that capacity and, therefore, the Rajinsama was binding on his brother Annaappa. [607 B C] (ii) The High court was in error in holding that theRajinama was a full relinquishment of the rights of both the brothers Shiddanna and Annaiah. [707 C] In the present case, the appellants did not purport to file, the same on behalf of Annappiappa nor had he any right to do so. [700 D] (iii) The appellants did nothing more than seek to enforce the rights conferred by the Rajasama. The appellants were not entitled to enforce their rights under the Rajisama. [ 700 E] (iv) The fact that the respondents had not filed a written statement and the evidence in support of their claim to an interest in the property was not sufficient to establish that the respondent had acted as karta. [600 G] (v) The respondents were not bound to file the same.

The respondent, a manufacturer of carbon paper, was assessed to sales tax at the rate of 2 per cent prescribed for unclassi fied goods and not at the rates specified in the Schedule to the Notification. The Sales Tax Officer, (Section IV), Kanpur, did not accede to the contention of the respondent that carbon paper did not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that ribbon was a part of the typewriter. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% and ribbon at 10%. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the levy. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that carbon papers did not lost its character because they were not paper as defined in the Act or the Rules and that the word 'paper ' in the Notification was not a part or a part thereof. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The word ' paper ' in Entry 2 of the Schedule is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. [838C] (2) The mere fact that the words 'paper" are used for bearing, writing or printing, or for packing, or in the same way, ribbon is not a decisive of its question whether a typewriter ribbon has been a part and a diesel is a part. [889D] (3) The expression 'paper other than hand made paper ' is not conclusive of the fact that carbon Paper is not paper. [869E] (4) The words 'popular sense ' in common parlance, are used in the sense of 'popsular sense. The word "paper" in the common parlance or in a commander sense means paper which is used for printing, writing, or printing or for drawing on, or by way of decorating, or cover ing the walls. [879F] (5) The use of the word " paper" in Entry 18 of the Second Schedule to that Notification is not determinative of the questions whether the articles are paper as commonly understood. The words "popical sense" in common dictionary, are not decisive. [899G] (6) The High Courts have rightly held that carbonpaper is not an accessory but an essen tial part of a typewriter. [909G H] (7) The fact that a word ' Paper ' forms part of an integral part of one of the type writer though it may not be possible to type out any matter without it. [919H] (8) The meaning of the words "paper other" in entry 2 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to, the Act is that the expression "paper " in the First Schedule to this Act includes paper which has been used for carrying out the purposes of the Act. [929A] (9) The term "paper ' is defined in section 2(g) of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 as meaning a sub stance which is meant for bearing writing, writing and printing. [939B] (10) The definition of "paper", in the U P. Sales tax Act, 1947, is wide enough to include paper which was used for making, writing etc. and also includes paper. The expression "popsical sense", in common usage, is used in a wide sense, meaning, of course, by the words, "pocular sense" and "paper".

The appellant was employed by the respondents 1 to 4 as a Manager of the appellant Mills at Amroha. On February 2, 1955, the General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents I to 4 from service on the ground that they had disobeyed the order of the management. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order on the grounds, inter alia, that the order was illegal and that the management had no right to transfer the respondents to any of its concerns in any place and the respondents were properly dismissed by the management, and that as the respondents had disobeying the order, they were properly dismiss ed by the appellant. The High Court held that the appellant had no locus standi to transfer an employee from one concern to another and that, as the respondent had disobey ed his order of transfer, they could not be transferred to another concern. The question for decision was whether the appellant was entitled to transfer him from one of his concerns to another. Held, that in the circumstances of the case, the appellant could not claim the right to the transfer of the respondents from one company to another, because, the respondent was not a party to the contract of service between the appellant and the respondent. The fact that the respondent did not have the right of transfer to another company does not prevent the employer to transfer his employee if he has the right under the contract to transfer it to another Company. The essential distinction between that case and the present one is that there the bank with its branches was one unit and the records clearly indicated that transfer was one of the ordinary incidents of service in the Bank. The respondent was a workman within the meaning of section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The definition of "workman" in section 2 (s) is wide enough to include a person who has been employed by an employer in any one of its concern. It is not necessary that the employer should be a person employed by him in any particular concern. In the present case, as it was not an express term of the contract between the parties, the respondents could not transfer the appellant from one unit to another of his in the facts of the present cases. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside the finding of the State Industrial Tribunal, as there was no express agreement between the respondent and the appellant, that it was a condition of service of employment of the respondent either express or implied that the employee had the right, to transfer them to any place where the business of the employer in the same line was situated, unless there was an express condition to the contrary in the contract.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948. The Employees ' State Insurance Corporation Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for certain benefits to employees in the case of factories or establishments situated in areas in which the provisions of both Chapters IV and V are in force. The Act was enacted in 1948 and the provisions thereof were made applicable to the employees in factories or establishment situated in any area in which they were in force, and the payment of contribution for that purpose was made by the employer under the or other similar payment or benefit under various other social welfare legislations. The appellant company claimed that the contribution payable under Chapter V A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The High Court held that the contributions payable under the Act were a fee, and its imposition was illegal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the payment made by it under Chapter IV A was not a fee but a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contribution payable by the appellant under Chapter VI A is a fee. It is not a tax. It has no legal protection. It does not require any service to be rendered by the employees and through them on the employer, in due course, when the scheme becomes fully operative in all areas. [1088G H] 2. The payment of special contribution under Chapter VII A by the employers under the , is a tax and not a fees. The Government cannot go on levying employers ' contribution under section 28 of the Act. [1188B] 3. The expression 'fee ' in section 28 is wide enough to include all taxes which may be levied by the Parliament, by the Legislature of any State and by both. It would be difficult for the legislature to decide in what areas and in respect of which factories the Employees 'State Insurance Corporation should be established. [1108C] 4. The scheme is confined to a few areas and though special contribution is levied from all employers wherever they be, in the cases of employers who straightaway receive the benefits of the insurance scheme, their rate of contribution is lower. [111D] 5. The object of the scheme is to provide a fund known as the Employees State Insurance Fund which is to be utilised for the benefits to be given to the workers under the . The cost of these benefits will not be met from the general revenues of the state, but will be borne entirely from the aforesaid fund only. [112E] 6. The provisions of Chapter VA of the , are in respect to matters enumerated in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The State Legislature has enacted the . In the vary nature of things, it would have been impossible for the Legislature to decide whether in what area and in relation to which factories or Establishments situate in areas where the provisions are not in force and the payments of contribution are made by employers who alone receive the benefit of the Insurance Scheme, their rates of contribution being higher while in the Case of employers, who do not yet receive the same benefits of insurance scheme. [113E F] 7. The Legislature of a State has enacted a . The Act is not intended to be a tax or a fee or a tax but it has been so laid down in argument that the benefit should not be indirect and remote. The reference, there to indirectness and remoteness was not made in connection with any delayed benefit from the point of view of time, but with reference to the very benefit itself and its connection with the levy. [114F G] 8.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. Their demands are of regularisation and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as the regular workers. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there is no work for them. The respondents are also running in heavy losses during the last three years and it is not possible to absorb the petitioners immediately as regular workmen. The petitioners have also filed a counter affi davit. The High Court rejected the petitioners ' claim. Hence this petition for special leave to appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petition, the Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment of equal pay for the period during which the same work is taken from him is purely on humanitarian ground so far. [610C] 2. The principles of regularisation are not applicable to the case of the petitioners. The doctrine of regularisation is not applicable in the case where the daily rated worker is doing the same job as the regularly employed workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay. [625E] 3. The concept of regularisation has not been applied in the instant case. The petitioner is not regular employees, they do not have any specific job to do, they are surplus to the establishment and merely kept on the roll on humanitarian basis. The respondent No. 2 is prepared to give benefit of the same even to those who may not have agitated their claim. [710C D] 4. The plea of regularisation does not arise. The question of directing their absorption and regu larisation does not arises. The Court has not found any ground to interfere with the High Court 's decision in view of the clear findings supported by evidence that there are no vacancies or work available in the establishment for absorption of the peti tioners and that for quite some time they have been continuing on rolls and paid in spite of there being no work available for them, they cannot be regularised and their retention on the rolls is purely purely on sympathetic grounds so far as. the petitioners are concerned. [650E F] 5. The claim of regularisation cannot be sustained. The writ petition must, therefore, fail.

The appellants purchased the entire 16 as interest in the property at a Court sale in pursuance of a decree obtained by them against Kazi Mohammed Ismail, the eldest son of Azam Ali. The appellants contended that the sale in execution of the mortgage decree obtained in pursuance thereof was not the sole proprietor or owner of the property and that the co heirs were estopped from questioning the validity of the sale. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appellants were precluded by 0. r. 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure from questioning their validity. The plaintiffs appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in holding that the plaintiffs were precluded from questioning its validity. [213 B] (ii) The proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial Court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the transaction on the evidence already on the record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale under exhibit 12(i) were held to be real, the plaintiffs would be entitled to a decree for a declaration that in addition to the 8 pies share granted to them by the High Court, they would be entitle to a further 2 as. 13 gondas odd share belonging to Ismail. [214 C D] (iii) The appellants ' contention that the property conveyed by exhibit 12 (i), was not a part of the estate of the deceased, was not correct. The sale in favour of the appellants was not made out and was not therefore void. [212 E] (iv) The sale was not for the benefit of the plaintiffs and the sale was for the purpose of the Court sale. [211 G] (v) The plaintiffs ' claim was not based on any evidence. The suit was not barred by 0 r. I of the Civil Procedure Code. [210 C] (vi) The suit could not be dismissed as frivolous.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 201 of Indian Penal code. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the acquittal and convicted him. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been complied with, and that as a necessary consequence of those omissions, the entire proceedings and the trial were vitiated. HELD : (i) The provisions of section 173(1) of Code of criminal Procedure have not been strictly complied with. The omission on the part of the police officer to fully comply with the provisions Of section 173, should not be allowed to have such a far reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective. [293 B] (ii) The omission to comply with section 173 of the Criminal Procedure Code, in order to simplify the procedure in respect of inquiries leading upto a Sessions trial, and at the same time to safeguard the interests of accused persons by enjoining upon police officers concerned and magistrates before whom such proceedings are brought, to see that all the documents, necessary to give the accused persons all the information for the proper conduct of their defence, are furnished. [294 E] (iii) The words "shall" occurring both in sub section (4) of section 207A and sub section(3), of section 208A are not mandatory but directory.
