The word "shall", occurring both under sub section 3 and section 207 A, is not mandatory and only directory, because an omission by a police officer, to fully complied with the provision of section 174, should be allowed, to have the same far reaching effects as to rendering the proceedingsincluding the trial in the court. [295 G H] (iv) The word 'shall ' occurring both sub section 4 and section 208 A, are not directory, but only directory.

The respondent Municipality was constituted under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888. The appellant was the owner of a factory and the respondent Municipality had been authorised to carry on the business of manufacturing and selling of sugar. The respondent Municipality issued a notice to the appellant under section 153A of the Act calling upon him to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in the manner specified in the notice. The notice was served on the appellant on the ground that the appellant had failed to comply with the requisition. The Special Officer held that the existence of a nuisance was a matter for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality and beyond the scope of his enquiry. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The scheme under section153A of Act is to leave it to the subjective opinion of the municipality as to the existence or existence of the nuisance in terms of sub section (1) of section 153 A of the Bombay Municipalities Act, 1925. The scheme of section153 A is to permit the Municipality, if it is satisfied that a nuisance in the terms of subsection (1), exists or not, to issue a notice requiring the person to whom the notice is issued to showcause why he shall not be ordered to arrange the discharge thereof in the way specified in such notice. [395 B C] (ii) The provisions of section 154A of Bombay Municipal Act, 1901 are not intended to be used for the purpose of preventing a nuisance which would affect the public health and fertility of the soil. The provisions are intended to prevent a nuisance. The purpose of the section is to prevent the nuisance which may affect the community health and the fertility or the fertile of the water. The provision is intended to protect the public from being polluted by the nuisance. [396 C D] (iii) The purpose for which the notice has been issued is to enable the Municipality to discharge the effluent into the premises of the factory. The Municipality is not required to give any notice to any person who is in charge of the premises. The Municipal Commissioner is not bound to give notice to a person who has been authorised by the Municipality. The procedure prescribed by section 153 is not followed.

The appellant was found in possession of railway stores which were not railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The appellant was convicted under section 3 of the Act and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution must first adduce evidence to show that there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. HELD: (i) The prosecution must also prove that the articles were being actually used or were intended to be used for the construction or operation of a railway. [189 D] (ii) The burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some peculiarity of the goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods. [190 E] (iii) The evidence in the case did not establish that the goods were railway stores. The prosecution was not called upon to prove that they were intended for the purpose of the construction, operation or maintenance of a Railway. [191 D] In the present case the prosecution was neither called upon nor was it asked to prove the articles seized. The evidence was not sufficient to prove this fact. [192 E] In most cases the burden of proving that the article belonged to any particular railway administration is not an offence. The burden in respect of this is discharged by the prosecution that the items were being used or intended to been used in the construction. [195 G] (iv) The appellant failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession of the articles. The report was not a mere statement to the effect that the contents of the report were correct.

The appellants filed a suit for ejectment of the respondents on the ground that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the first appellate court. The High Court reversed the decree of the trial Court and decreed the suit for eviction. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Amending Act does not apply to the facts of the case. The Legislature intended that the heirs of the tenants of commercial premises will cease to enjoy the protection afforded to the tenant under the Act. [10E] 1.2 The legislature intended that heirs of tenants of residential premises will continue to enjoy protection afforded by the Act and also subject to the rights in favour of the respond ent created under section 13(1) (a) to (k) and other provi sions of the Act, and also Subject to the right in favour o f the responde nt created under Section 13(2) (i) to the extent provided in Section 13 (1) and alsosubject to the provisions of the Rent Acts. [11F] 1:3 The Legislature did not intend that the heir of the tenancy of the appellants will cease, to enjoy an estate or interest in the tenanted premises. [12F] 2.1 In the instant case, the tenancy rights are heritable and the heirs are entitled to enjoy them the protection of the provisions under the Rent Act. The heirs of such tenants are entitled only to enjoy their protection under the provisions. [13G] 2:2 The appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in a lease hold right in the demised property governed by the Rent laws not liable to be evicted as a matter of course under the ordinary law of the land and he is entitled to remain in possession even after determination of the contractual tenancy and no order or decree for eviction will be passed against a tenant unless any ground which entitles the landlord to get an order or judgment for possession specified in the Act is established. [14G] 3.1 Section 13 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 provides that a contractual tenant on the termination of the contract of tenancy is by virtue of the provision of the rent Acts not liable for eviction as a matters of course. The tenant who continues to remain In possession even before the termination or the contractual lease of the premises is terminated, continues to have an estate and interest in such tenanted premises and tenancy rights in respect of commercial tenancies are heritable. Therefore, despite the termination, the tenant continues to be in possession as on the date of the suit as statutory tenants. [15H; 16A] 3:3. The provisions of all the Rent Control Legislation are that a contract of lease is by way of a statutory tenancy and not by way or by way. The contractual tenancy is heritable and, therefore, the heirs and successors of the landlord are entitled for enjoy the benefit of the protection under section 2(1)(iii). [16B] 4.1. The legislature did not intended that in the case of residential tenancies after the termination o f tenancy of a tenant, as has been done in the cases of heirs of tenant, after termination of tenancy, as had been done by the tenant in the instant cases, the LegislatUre which has created this right has thought it fit in the ease of residential tenancy to limit the rights of the heirs in the manner and to the effect provided in section 13 (2) of the . [16C D] 4:2. The Amending Acts do not apply in the facts and circumstances of the instant ease. The tenants are not entitled to get the protection as they are not governed by any of the Acts.

The appellant Board was willing to extend the benefits of the Employees ' Provident Fund Act, 1952 to all the workers except the Government servants who were on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Scheme applies. The appellant Board had to pay the provident fund and gratuity to all its employees. The employees claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident Fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees' Provident Fund. The Tribunal held that the employees of the appellant Board should be given the same benefits and the same should be taken into consideration while deciding matters regarding benefits to be made available to its employees, and that the Board was not entitled to any additional benefits. The High Court in appeal held that there was no distinction in the matter of payment of provident fund scheme and that it would bring about serious injustice if they were deprived of their benefits under the Act, and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Board 'S Provident Fund is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserve. [47C] (2) The contribution to the provident Fund is an obligation and a definite percentage whereas it was open to the ordinary commercial concerns to credit some amount to its depreciation reserve, and the burden of provident Fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer. [48D] (3) The financial capacity of the employer is to be taken as a whole and not as a part of the fund. The contribution is a specific proportion whereas the same is open for an ordinary industrial concern to Credit any amount which is to the credit of any amount. [49E] (4) The contributions to the Provident Fund are a statutory obligations and are a definite ratio. The financial position of the industry as well as the fact that the burden is to pay provident fund, gratuity and provident fund can be met without undue strain on the financial position. [50F] (5) The amount to be provided for taxation and for development rebate reserve could not be deducted in order to ascertain the financial capacity. [51G] (6) The appellant 's contribution to provident fund is a Statutory obligation and was a definite share whereas it has been open to a ordinary commercial Concern to credit an amount to depreciation reserve and the balance sheet shows a very large amount in the shape of interest payable to the Government.

The respondent wife filed a petition for maintenance under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Magistrate dismissed the application filed by the respondent for maintenance. The High Court accepted the revision application of the respondent and set aside the order of the Magistrate and held that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with her husband. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the wife having been impotently impotence, this could not be a ground for refusing to live in the husband merely because her husband was impotant and unable to discharge his marital obligation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The decisions referred to above in the judgment taking a contrary view must be held to be no longer good law and are hereby overruled. [707B] 2. The decision in Arunachala Anandayammal vs Babu Lal Dixit, J. sounded a very pragmatic note on this aspect of the matter and in this connection pointed out that the scope of the Amendment of 1949 was not very much wider than that of the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125. [807C] 3. The Courts cannot compel the wife 's refusal to live without her husband 's consent. [907D] 4. The courts cannot compel a wife to stay with her in a situation where her physical and mental well being might be adversely affected, as there is no intention on the part of the husband to inflict that cruelty, she should suffer that predicament without demur and be satisfied with a grab to bite and some rags to clothe her and a roof over her head. [1007E] 5. The Court cannot compel an wife to live separately from her husband on the ground that the father though he is forcing her in the situation where she is impotable and unable, to discharge her marital obligation, this would not be just ground to refuse the wife, if she refused to live together with her father. [1107F] 6. The provisions of the Act are clear and unambiguous and are not intended to be used to defeat the object of the legislation. [1108G] 7. The object and interpretation of the two provisos to sub sections (3), (3A) and (3B) of Section 125 of Cr. P.C. is to ensure that the woman who is impetent and is unable to perform her marital obligations, is not to be a mere ground for refusal to maintain the wife. [111A] 8. The two provisos are not mutually exclusive and are intended to operate in different fields. The first proviso to Section 125(3) is a proviso to the old section which is also a proviso. The second proviso is a substantive provision and is not intended merely to be an exception to the main provision. [112B] 9. The words "in the case of a husband" in the proviso are wide enough to include a husband who has contracted marriage with another woman or keeps a mistress. The proviso is not a substantive one. The language of the proviso is clear and explicit. The intention of the legislature is clear that the legislature intended that the proviso should be construed in a manner which would advance the object and purpose of the enactment. [113C D] 10. The expression "in any case" in section 125(1) of the Cr.P.C., is not used to enlarge the scope and ambit of the main part of section 488 of the Criminal Procedure Code. [114D] 11. The word "in" in Section 125 (1) is not defined in the Code.

The plaintiff, a public limited company, was the owner of certain lands in the city of Bhavnagar. The State of Saurashtra, by virtue of the orders of the Government of Saurashtra dated 19th January, 1948, and 29th February, 1948 vested in the plaintiff the land of the suit property. The plaintiff claimed that the lands were vested in it by virtue Of the orders dated 19.1. 1948 and 29.2. 1948. The defendants denied the title of the plaintiff and contended that the suit was barred by limitation. The Trial Court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the plaintiff had not shown possession of the land as claimed by him and that the defendants had denied title of his plaintiff. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the vesting of the title in the Municipality was not intended to be vesting in its full amplitude, but was meant only to appoint the Municipality as agent of the State to dispose of the lands. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit was for possession based on title to the suit land and the defendants have denied title. The plaintiffs had also admitted that the structures in Rasala Lines were not shown to be that of the Municipality in the Municipal records and even in the plaint they did not claim the ownership of the property as stated in the letter of the government dated 10th August, 1965. [222B C] 2. The Resolution No. 37 dated 19 th January,1948 was only a right or an authorisa tion to sell the land. The resolution No. 77 dated 29th Feb. 1948 was only an authority to sell and take the income therefrom. The Government of India had corrected themselves in their communication dated 6th May, 1952 and stated that the claim of the plaintiffs that the land was vested in Bhavnagar Municipality was erroneous and that it was not necessary either to deal with the argument of the defendants that the vest was not recognised by the Union of India or the State Government and that therefore it was necessary for the Court to give a finding on title of plaintiff even if the defendants in possession had not pleaded adverse possession. [223D E] 3. The question whether the vesting was an act of the sovereign or sovereign character is a question of fact depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [224F] 4. The decision of the High Court that the possession of land was also not taken by the Municipali ty at any time, is not correct. [225G] 5. The finding of the Trial Court that possession of lands was also in the possession was not correct and that there could not be any legal possession with the plaintiff as the title to it was never recognised by Union ofIndia or the Government.

The appellant was a lessee of a village who had undertaken to keep an account of its forest revenue and pay a certain proportion to the Government, keeping the remainder for himself and the question whether he was an officer within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant was convicted under section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947 and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . The appellant contended that he was not an officer of the Government and was not employed to exercise any public duty and therefore was not a public servant within the definition of section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. Held, that the appellant was an "officer" within the terms of section 3 of the Act and was therefore a public servants within the scope of section 1(9). The appellant had been rightly convicted under the Act. The fact that he had been convicted as a public officer was not sufficient to attract the provisions of section 5 (1)(c) of that Act. In the present case, the appellant had not been employed to perform any public duties. The question whether a person was an 'officer ' within the term of section 20(9), Indian Penal code, was one which was not the subject matter of the present appeal. The word "officer " in section 21 of the Code of Criminal Procedure means "any person employed to do any public work". The appellant could not be said to be an officer in the service or pay of the government. The words "any officer in a service or paid of Government" in section 2(9)(a) of Indian Penal Act, are wide enough to include all railway servants. The expression "any other person employed" in the section means "a person employed in the execution of any public function". The word 'officer" in that section means a person employed by the Government to do a public duty. The definition of "officer ' in section 3(9A) of Bombay Act II Of 1947, is wide enough and includes all railway servant. The meaning of the word "Officer" in s.21 of the Penal Code is that any person employed or employed to discharge any public functions, whether by himself or by any other person, is in the employment or pay or of the State Government. The term "officer in the Service or pay" in cl. (9) is wide and includes a person who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty, and is therefore a "officer". The words 'any person ' in the definition are wide and include all persons employed in any public office. The dictionary meaning of "Officer " in the context of the definition is "any one who is employed to act in the discharge of any duty or obligation". The definition is wide in its amplitude and includes every person employed for the execution or performance of any work which is performed by him. The mere fact that a person is employed in a public office does not necessarily mean that he is employed by a person in the performance or performance or any other duty. It is not enough that a man should be in the pay or service of the Govt. and is also performing a public function. The distinction between a person and a person appointed to a public post is that he must be in a position to perform a public duties and that he should be paid a certain amount of money. The nature of the duties of a public functionary is not such as to make him a public Servant within the ambit of section 6(1) of Chapter II of the Bombay Act.

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala, for recovery of a sum of Rs.1,50,000/ as arrears of land revenue. The suit was decreed by the Sub Judge on the ground that the property attached and notified for sale was not exempt from attachment and sale under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Respondent filed an appeal to the District Judge, who dismissed the appeal. The High Court allowed the second appeal holding that the portion of the building in which the liquor shop was situated was exempt from attached and sale. The respondent then filed a second appeal before the High Court. The Division Bench of the High court allowed the appeal holding (i) that the part of the property in which liquor shop is situated was liable to attachment and sales under clause(ccc), and (ii) that it was exempt under clause.(ccc). The High court also held that the said portion of building was exempt by virtue of the provisions of section 61 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The attachment levied on and the auction sale notified in respect of the Respondent 's half share in the said property were not in execution of any decree of a civil court but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorized to adopt proceedings under the said Act for recovery. [848C] 2. The provisions of Section 60 of Code do not apply to an attachment and sell under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. The words "such attachment or sale" in the proviso refer to the attachment and the sale mentioned in sub section(1) thereof. The expression "such attached or sale " in the aforesaid proviso refers to the attached and sold mentioned in subsection (1). The attachment imposed on and auction sale of the respondent 's share in that property was not in pursuance to the order passed by an Officer authorized to take proceedings under that Act for recovering revenue due to the State. [884D E] 3. The properties, if any, which are exempt from the attachment or sales in revenue recovery proceedings under section 60, would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said act. [874E] 4. The property, if my, which is exempt from sale and sale in revenue Recovery proceedings under this Act would be merely such properties which are so exempt by the aforesaid Act. [864G] 5. The attached property was, therefore, not exempt under section 61.

The respondent, a displaced person, filed a suit for declaration that the lands in question were acquired by the Government under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had failed to prove that the acquired lands were not his own lands and that the value of the lands was not the correct market value. The High Court, however, held that the valuation of the acquired land was not correct and that it was not a case of mistake apparent from the record and as such the impugned notice was liable to be quashed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that there had been escapement of assessment to duty because the lands were undervalued in view of the glaring enhanced compensation awarded by the Civil Court and the High court 's decision upholding the issuance of such notice on the wrong basis was liable for be set aside. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent had merely accepted the value as determined by the Special Deputy Collector in his award and the accountable person had no objection to this course and, therefore, the enhanced compensation was sought to be included in the principal value of estate by undertaking the rectification proceedings. [334B] 2. The impugned notice issued under s.61 of the Act on the basis that the land still formed part of the estate of the deceased and that having regard to the glaring increase in compensation awarded, the said lands had been undervalued in the original assessment and as a result thereof the said land had escaped assessment to tax. [330C] 3. The notice issued by the respondent on the correct assumption that the acquisition lands still formed parts of the state of thedeceased which passed on his death, that the market value of those lands adopted on the earlier occasion which was on the date of the death of the respondent, was not in existence at the date when the original assessments were made, was liable only to be setaside. [328D] 4. The question whether the respondent was entitled to compensation for the lands acquired by it was a question of fact and the same was not raised in the High Courts. [332F] 5. The expression "the market value" in section 61 of the Land Acquis tation Act, is wide enough to include the market price of the land acquired by a Government. The word "market value" is not defined in the Act. The definition of "market Value" in the Land Act is wide and includes the market rate of the property acquired by an owner. [333G] 6. The words "market price" in Section 61 of Land Acqi tion Act are wide enough and include the price of land acquired for the purpose of determining the market valuation. The market value is the price which a willing purchaser would pay to a willing seller for the property. The price paid by a willing vendor for the land is the market rent which a prudent purchaser would receive from the willing seller. [336C] 7. The value of a land acquired under the Act is the fair market value on the day of the acquisition. The land acquired is the property of the Government. [340D] 8. The compensation awarded to the respondent is not a proper evaluation of the right to receive compensation as on the dates of the original assess ment under section 73 A of the . [335E] 9. The determination of market value by the civil court is not final and conclusive. The civil court has no jurisdiction to determine the marketvalue of the properties acquired by Government. It is only the market rates of the said properties which are to be determined by a civil court. [341F] 10. The valuation of lands acquired under section 36 of the is not the proper valuation of any land acquired.

The appellant was elected as a Director of the Bank from the Brehmapuri Agricultral Sales and Purchase Society. The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986 and he was elected on 18.8.1986 as one of the Directors of the bank from the said Brehma Puri Agricultrial Sales and purchase Society. On 8.1.1987, the District Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur, issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors of a Cooperative Society and why he be not removed from his office as Director or Executive Committee Member of the Executive Committee of a Co operative Society and u/s 73FF(2) of Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act 1960, and directed him to remain present on 2.2.1987 at 11.00 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office. The Deputy Registrar, Cooperative Societies by his order dated 7.12.1987 removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Deputy Registrar removing the appellant as Director of a cooperative society and the High court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The disqualification as a defaulter continued after the election of the appellant and section 78 envisaged such a default and the appellant having continued to be a defaulter was lawfully removed and the fact that he repaid the loan before the notice was issued would not be material for the purpose of taking action under section 79(1). [680B] 1.2 The disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18.08.1986 to 21.10.1986 was extinguished and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. [680C] 1:3. The disqualification in the case of term lending society, a member who defaults the payment of any instalment of the loan granted to him, is not a defaulter in presenti on the date of the notice and the provisions of section 78 are not attracted. [679D] 1 :4. The word 'shall ' in section 78 of the Act has to be interpreted in the context of the provisions in the section. [681E] 1(a) The word "shall" in section 79 of the is used in the sense of "shall". The word shall" in the said section is used to mean "shall", and the word "may" in that section is not used in any other sense. [682F] 1.(b) The expression "shall ' has been used in section 77 of the Bombay Cooperative Societies Rules, 1960. The words "shall be deemed to be vacant" in Section 78 of that Act are not used to denote the word 'may '. [683F] 2.1 In the instant case, the notice of the Assistant Registrar was in effect to say that the appellant had already ceased to be the Director and his seat already fell vacant. This has to he interpreted in context of section 77. [684G] 2:2. The notice of Deputy Registrar was not in effect a defaulter and the disqualification continued after election of appellant and Section 78 envisaged a separate procedure for calling in question the appellant 's election as a director. [685F] 3.1 Section 78(2), which is a special provision for setting aside an election must prevail over section 78 as there would be apparent conflict between the two and the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, would apply, and the mere making of payment on 21.

The respondent was in the service of the State of Maharashtra as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. The State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government 'S order dated December 4 1982 reducing his pension by 50% permanently under rule 188 of Bombay Civil Service Rules. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Government has power to reduce the amount payable to a Government servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service. [34G] 2. The reduction of pension by fifty per cent was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the respondent. [35A] 3. The order reducing the pension by 100 per cent is too harsh, disproportionate to his misconduct proved. [36B] 4. The impugned order reducing pension by 25 per cent would seriously affect his living. [37C] 5. The provisions of Rule 189 of the Rules are not applicable to the instant case as in the present case the purpose of the enquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent 's pension. The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of Bombay civil Services Rules, and the State government had power to reduced the pension payable by 50 percent.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 3(3) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 (U.P.) was invalid in law. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the order of the Commissioner was invalid and that the appellant 's suit was incompetent. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts were not justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the revisional power conferred on the Commissioner by section 3 (3). [563 E] (ii) The words of section 3 are clear and unambiguous and they indicate that the jurisdiction of the civil courts is completely excluded in relation to the question as to whether permission has been properly or validly granted or refused by the appropriate authorities exercising their powers under the relevant provisions of the Act. [563 F] (iii) The word 'may ' in section 3 of the , is not defined in the Act and it is not necessary that the Commissioner should have given notice to the tenant before he can make an order. The word "may" in section 2(3), is not used in the sense of a mandatory provision. The words "may", in section 4(1) are clear enough to indicate that it is intended to confer wide jurisdiction on the commissioner. [562 G H] (iv) The Commissioner can deal with the question whether permission had been properly granted or not. The fact that the Act did not intend to confer any wide jurisdiction upon the Commissioner, would not make the order wholly invalid and as such, a nullity. [564 B] (v) The provisions of section 4 (1) of U. P. ( Temporary) Control Act, 1948, do not intend, even prior to the amendment of 1954, to limit the jurisdiction to the Commissioner only to cases where irregularity or illegality has been committed by the District Magistrate in granting or refusing permission. [565 C] (vi) The fact, however, that the provisions of sections 3 (4) and 16 of the Uttar Pradesh (Temporary Control of Eviction) Act, 1950, do indicate that they intended to give wide jurisdiction to a Commissioner only in cases where the District Magistrates have acted illegally or with material irregularity or has wrongly refused to act, is a nullity and it existence should be ignored by the civil court.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was appointed as a member by the Punjab State Public Service commission. He was removed from his office by an order of the President on the ground of misbehaviour. The appellant challenged the order of removal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order was vitiated by the non compliance with the provisions of article 317(1) of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of dismissal was not vitiated by any non compliance of the provisions contained in article 317 (1) and the order passed by the President was not in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under article 317. [642C] 2. The question whether the order is vitiated by non compliance or non compliance is a matter which has to be decided by the Court of first instance. [643E] 3. The power of the Governor to make a reference to this court under article 318(1), is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article provides that the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commissions can only be removed from office on the grounds of misbehaviour and (ii) the order cannot be passed after the Supreme Court has on inquiry reported to the President that the person concerned is guilty of misconduct and, secondly, whether the misconduct is of such a nature as to require his removal from the office of Member of the Public Service Commis sion. [641C D] 4. The fact that the evidence of any particular witness is recorded by the learned Judge will not conclude the issue as regards the admissibility or relevance of that evidence. [651D] 5. The mere fact that a witness has not filed an affidavit in this Court will not be conclusive to decide the Reference on a consideration of the affidavits only. [631E] 6. The Court will, therefore, record the evidence which the parties lead before him, within the constraints of the following guidelines: (1 ) The affidavits filed in this court will be treated as the examination in chief of the respective witnesses. (2) The evidence to be recorded by a Judge will be limited to the cross examination of witnesses who have filed affidavits before the Court. [661F] 7. The evidence will be transmitted to the Registrar (Judicial) of this Court immediately after the entire evidence is recorded.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act No. Chatterjee, for the recovery of certain amounts from the respondents. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the approach made by the High Court was wholly incorrect and it has misconstrued the evidence and documents produced in the case to show that the endowment was of a public nature. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question as to whether the endowment is of a private nature or of a Public nature has to be decided with reference to the facts proved in each case and it is difficult to lay down any test or tests which may be of universal application. [833C] 2. The mere fact that members of the public used to come to the temple with out any hindrance, does not necessarily mean that the temple is a public temple. [ 833D] 3. The fact that the members of a community used to take offerings from the members or their descendants, does no necessarily mean, that the deity was a public endowment. [820E] 4. The existence of a family deity in the temple by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the member of the community had a right to worship in the Temple. [821F] 5. The nature of the endowment would be to find out if the management of the property dedicated is in the hands of the strangers or members of their family. [822G] 6. The evidence shows that the founder of the temple was merely to instal a family idol in the deity. The factum of worship would not determine the nature of endowment. It is manifest that whenever a dedication is made for religious purposes and a deity installed in a temple, the worship of the deity is a necessary concomitant of the installation of the idol, and therefore, the mere factum of worshipping the temple would not be a conclusive proof to show the private nature of such endowment. The only inference that can be drawn from the evidence is that the dedication was of the private character. [823G H] 7. The finding of the High court that the endowments were of a purely charitable nature and the intention of the founder was merely a circumstance which may in some cases conclusively establish that the trust was of such a nature. [825A] 8. The burden of proving that the property was of public nature is on the person who asserts the right to the worship. The onus is on him to prove that the public has a right of worship in a particular temple. The presumption is not a mere possibility of the existence of the trust. [826B] 9. The position of a trustee in a private endowment is different from that of a person who has no interest in the property. The distinction between the nature and character of a trust is that one of the important tests to determine the character of the dedication is to find whether the user of the Temple by members of public or in the hand of the members thereof or their ancestors, is a clear proof of the intention to dedicate the temple to public and not to the members. [827C D] 10. The test is whether the dedication of the institution by members is of public character. The essence of the right is that it is a private one. The intention of a founder is merely to dedicates the temple for the benefit of the family or their families. The words "public" and "public endowment" are not defined in the Act. [828G H; 834A] 11. The word "public trust" is not defined under the Act but it is used in the sense of a religious endowment.

The appellant Bank was a contractor to the military and other authorities. The appellant Bank entered into certain contracts with the Government in respect of the supply of certain goods to the respondent. The respondent was the agent of the appellant Bank. The contract was to be executed by the appellant on July 13, 1946. The agreement was to come into force on July 19, 1948. The terms of the contract were that the appellant would pay to the Bank out of the monies receivable under the bills and other amounts and to receive the amount thereof and appropriate such receipts towards and in repayment of the advances made or to be made hereafter and all other monies due from the appellant to the attorneys in any account whatever. The document was executed on July 14, 1946 and the appellant was authorised to sue for recovery and receive the monies due in connection with the contracts with approval of MaLhotra. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The High Court held that the power of attorney was irrevocable and that the document was brought into existence in connection therewith. The appeal to this Court was filed by the Bank on the ground that the Power of attorney dated July 13 1946 was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant bank out of a specific fund of the borrower in the hands of the Government authorities. HELD : (i) The power of Attorney coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19 1948 was a valid one. The power conferred on the attorney coupled with endorsement on it was a conditional one. [782 E] (ii) The document executed by Malhotra was a complete engagement by the borrower to pay him out of his assets in the hand of the government authorities. [777 G] (iii) The agreement dated July 14 1946 was not a valid agreement. The letter dated July 18, 1948 was not an equitable assignment of the moneys due under the bill in favour of the respondent and was irrevocable. [779 C] (iv) The appellant bank was merely authorised to act as his agent. The endorsement on bill dated August 19, 1949 created an interest in a specific Fund and was unconditional. [780 D] (v) The letter of the attorney dated August 13, 1948 created an equitable assignmen of the fund by way of security. The order of attorney coupledwith the endorsement thereon was a clearly engagement by Malayalam to pay to Bharat Bank Ltd., Jabalpur.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd. The said company had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. The assessee was an employee of the managing agent of M.L.A. and was paid his salary as defined in section 17 of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner. But on further appeal to the Tribunal, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits in lieu of salary, the same was exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3) (ii). The High Court answered the question in the negative and in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary. [440C] The receipt in the present case is not salary and the same cannot be said to be either interest on the securities. The receipt is undoubtedly an income. [441F] The receipts of Rs 27,949/ by M. L.A., are dealt with by section 16. [442F] In defining the expression "Profits in lieu" the legislature excluded from the scope of that expression any payments received by the assesee from a provident fund, his own contributions to the fund or any interest on such contributions.

The petitioners who were the owners of certain cattle, were carrying on their respective trades. They were prosecuted under section 3(1) (a) (i) of the Bihar Act, 1950, for having committed an offence under section 4(1)(a) of that Act. The petitioners contended that the Act violated article 19(1), (g) and (h) of Constitution and that the impugned Act was void as it contravened article 19 (1) of ' the Constitution. Held, that the provisions of the Act were not violative of article 19 of the Constitution and the impugned Acts were not saved by article 19. The impugned Acts did not infringe the fundamental rights of the petitioners under article 19, and were therefore void. The Act was not saved from the operation of article 31(2) of Part III of the constitution. The provisions of section 3 (1)(b) of Bihar Act were valid and the Act was valid. The Bihar Act was constitutionally valid in so far as it prohibited the slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of cows and calve of cows, male and female, and was therefore void in so insofar as it prohibits the slaughter Of cows of any ages and Calves of buffaloes, male or female, but that it was void in respect of the slaughter. The entire provision banning the slaughter was valid and was in consonance with the directive principles laid down in article 48 of the Consti tution. The whole provision baning the slaughter and the slaughter were valid.

The respondent was a public limited company having its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh. The Company was incorporated in the State of Madhya Pradesh and its Manager was appointed as an employee of the Company. The respondent was employed as an Assistant Manager in the Company and was paid a salary of Rs. 500 per month. The company was also a public company. The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The name and ticket number of the respondent were not included in the departmental muster. The question for determination was whether the respondent was an employee within the meaning of the Standing Orders. Held, that the respondent had committed a breach of the statutory provision in section 30 of the local Act in the sense that no Standing Orders had been made in respect of the appellant company and the respondent did not fulfil the necessary condition of having his name and tickets number included in it. The word "employee" in the definition clause means such categories of employees as may from time to time be declared to be workmen by the management and Standing Order No. (e) of Standing Order, No. 1, which was applicable to the respondent, and the expression "employee " in the Standing Order was not an essential characteristic of an employee. The essential content of the definition of an 'employee ' is employment in the Office, Mains Department, eta., of the company either at Nagpur or Wardha, and that of a workman the necessary declaration by the Company which would entitle him to a ticket under Standing Order NO. (f) of the standing Orders, and, therefore, the respondent who had no ticket was outside his purview, and as the respondent could not fulfil this essential condition of being an employee, the appellant was not entitled to a certificate under section 30.

The appellant company was an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by a Government Company. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The Tribunal held that alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this Project went into production. The appellant company contended that the Alloy Steel project was a composite establishment and could not be treated as a separate unit for purposes of section 16 of the Act. The Company contended that alloys steel Project was an establishment which had been in existence for a long period and had been even earning profits, so, that exemption could not he granted to this Company in respect Of payment of bonus under section 16. The company also contended that it was not a separate Establishment because under the Act, a company is itself an establishment, so as to be treated separately for the purpose of computation of bonus. The tribunal held that the alloy steel Project could not, be treated to be a separate entity because under section 3 of the , the Company was itself an 'establishment ' and could be treated only as a part of the main establishment owned by Hindustan Steel Ltd. and that the proviso to section 3 will not apply in such a case. The High Court held that even though alloy Steels Project was owned, managed and managed, by Hindustan steel Ltd., it had to be regarded as a distinct establishment for purposes Of section 16(1) of the . The High court also held that there was no evidence at all that in any year, after Alloy steel project was set up bonus was paid to the employees of all the units on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units. The appeal by special leave was filed by the appellant company against the decision of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that merely because Alloy Steels project was owned controlled and controlled by Hindustan Iron Ltd., the principal part of section 3 would apply and all such departments, undertakings or branches must be treated together as parts of one single establishment for purpose of computing bonus under the . [657 D] (2) The proviso to sub section (2), of section16 only comes in the way it is bonus is paid in any years to the employee of all units on that basis. [658 E] (3) The Explanation to sub s.(2) of section 15 only comes into the way of the claim, because there is no evidence that in some year, before Alloy Iron Project was setup bonus was given to the workmen of all those units on a consolidated profits. [613 F] (4) The expression "any other establishment" in section 3 cannot be used in a narrow sense. It is not possible to accept the contention that the expression "other establishment" is used in the sense of a separate and distinct establishment.

The appellant, a sugar mill, was manufacturing sugar from sugar cane. The cess was payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act. The appellant challenged the levy of cess on the ground that the sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Cess Act. It was contended that the cess was not payable by the appellant as it was not a 'vegetable ' in Item (6) of Schedule 1 to the cess Act. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The word 'veg etable ' has been used in Entry 15 in Schedule I of the Cess Rules. The expression 'vegeable ' is generally understood to mean as bringing into existence a new substance and does not mean 'merely ' to produce some change in a sub stance, however minor in consequence, the change may be. [529G H] 2. The term 'veetable ' means product of or made of or out of vegetable. [525A] 3. The words 'vetable ' and 'veotable ' are not products of manufacture unless they are understood in common parlance and it must be given its popular sense meaning. The dictionary meaning of the word 'vesgetable" is not a word of the widest amplitude. The definition of 'veegetable product ' in Entry No. 15 of the Schedule I is wide enough to include 'vets of vegetable products '. [500B C] 4. The sugar manufacturing industry does not, therefore, come within the ambit of Entry 15. [429C] 5. The Sugar manufacturing industry do not, however, come under Entry 15 and a fortio ri the manufacture of alcohol from molasses could not be considered to be an industry within Entry No 15. The 'vellable product" means product or made out of or in any other form of vegetable, and is not an industry for certain purposes and vegetables are products of that industry. [511D] 6. The meaning of 'vessels ' is not to be given the meaning of vegetables which are kept on the dining tables for dinner purposes, and it has a wider amplitude. [629E] 7. The expressions 'vexable ' or 'veilable ' have been used as a verb in common sense and it is not possible to give the meaning to the word "vegetables" in Entry 14 of Schedule l of the Act, because the word is generally used in the context in which it is occurring and to the fitness of the matter to the statute. [550F G] 8. The use of the expression 'vesltable product or 'silk ' in the definition of "vegable product " in Entry 18 of Schedule 11 of the Central Excise Act, 1944, is not decisive. The fact that the word has been employed in the sense in which the word was used in a particular industry in the present case does not attract the botanic meaning. [552G H; 553A] 9. The question for consideration is whether the industry manufacturing sugar itself is an industry as defined in the Act and a 'vesllable ' product ' means products of or make of or is made of, or out from vegetable. The contention that the expression "vetables" has been given a wider meaning and it cannot be given a meaning of vegetable as referring to any and every kind of plant life is to be taken to be a industry within the meaning Of Entry 15, is rejected.

The respondent, an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant on the ground that he required the premises for the purpose of carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the practice of the profession of an Advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3) (a) (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the use of the expression 'business ' in Section 10 (3) of Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1961, was not a business within section 10(1) (i) of that Act and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of his tenant on the grounds of his requirement unless it was for the purposes of carrying out his profession. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression ' business ' in section 10 (1) of Act, is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or profession of a lawyer. [14D] 2. The word 'business" in section 2(a) of A.P. Buildings ( Lease, Rent & Eviction) Act is used to include a profession of lawyers. The words 'business of a profession ' are used in the context of the statute in which it occurs and not in the sense of the word 'profession '. [15E F] 3. The term 'business " in section 5(3)(a)(iii) is used for the limited purpose of the Act. The definition of 'business in section 3(a)(ii) is wide enough to include any profession. [16F] 4. The use of expression 'profess ' in the Andhra Act is not a restricted one. The meaning of the term 'professed ' in that Act is to include all the provisions of the Acts including section 4 which provides for the determination of fair rent and section 10 which bars the eviction from a non residential building where the landlord is not occupying a nonresidential building in a city town or village concerned which is his own or to the possession of which he is entitled whether under the Act or otherwise. [17F G] 5. The phrase 'business carried on by a lawyer ' in s.10(3), is used as a wide meaning so as not to include an profession. The legislature has used the expression "business" as a wider meaning so that the word may have when it occurs in other statutory provisions. [18F G; 19A] 6. The concept of business is not confined to the business of a professional or a doctor. The profession of professional is not the carrying on of a trade or business within s. 10(2)(a) and the word "business ' has to be construed in the light of the context in which the statute occurs and cannot be given a wide interpretation so as, to include such practice. [19F G]. 7. The question whether the practice is a 'business within the definition of section 10 of the A. P. Buildings Act, 1950, is a question of fact. The respondent was a professional and was not carrying on any profession within the ambit of section 2 (a)(i) (ii) of this Act. [20F G H] 8. The appellant was a practising Advocate. He was not in possession of any residential building in the city town. He had no business in the town. The business of the advocate was not carried on in the City town. It was not the business which was carried on for the business. The practice of law was 'business. [21F G, 22A] 9.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for the recovery of Rs. 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The appellant contended that the respondent was not a debtor to the respondent for the approximate sum of Rs 4,00,000 and that the suit was barred by time. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the use of the word 'deposit ' by itself occurring either in the roznamcha or in the letter dated 29 September 1942 written by Ram Ratan Gupta would not be decisive of the question whether it was a case of deposit of the sum of money by the respondent with the appellant under an agreement that the same would be paid on demand. The respondent appealed to this Court. HELD : The High Courts were right in holding that there was a demand for a part of the amount in the year 1943 because the history of the transactions between the appellant and the respondent showed that the appellant had to be put on a footing of financial stability by giving the appellant the use Of the sum. The letter further shows that the terms were agreed to by the partners of the firm, namely, the partners. The agreement was between the parties. The transaction was between them and the appellant. The payment of Rs 5,00000 was debited to India Supplies. The amount was debited in the account of the respondent. The fact that the amount was credited to India Supply would not make the respondent liable for the amount. [575 D E] The High court was right in its view that there must be an unqualified demand for the whole sum before the limitation can star in case of demand for return of the money deposited.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, dated February 28, 1986, made in exercise of powers vested under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The petitioner made an application to this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution for quashing the order of detention. The petition was dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal to this court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order was passed by an authority not competent to pass an order of preventive detention and that the detaining authority was not satisfied that the petitioner was likely to get bail, and that there was no warrant for the detention of the detenu. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu is already in custody does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining author ity in making an order under the National Security Act. [845C] 2. The detaining authority is aware of the fact that he was already in detention and yet he was sub jectly satisfied that his detention was necessary. [ 845D] 3. The question whether a detention order can be passed against a person in jail is a matter of jurisdition but has to be decided on the facts of each case. [820E] 4. The detenu is not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. The order of the detention is liable to be quashed. [821F] 5. The detention order is liable for the same reasons as in the instant case. The grounds of detention are not vague and indefinite. The only ground on which the detention order was made is that the person was already under detention. It is not a matter which can be decided by the detaining Authority in making the order. [822F] 6. The facts of the present case show that the detention was in fact in the custody of the authority when the order is made. The Court, therefore, held that the fact of the detenue being in custody when the detention came to be made, yet he had been satisfied that he had already been in custody and yet the order could not be passed. [823G H] 7. The law laid down by this Court in Rameshwar Shaw 's case is that merely on the ground that an accused in jail has been acquitted, the appeal is pending and in re spect of which he may be granted bail may not in all circumstances entitle an authority to direct preventive detention. [824A B] 8. The mere fact that a detenu is in custody is not taken away the jurisdition of the Detaining Authority in passing an order for preventive detention, and the principle enunciated by the aforesaid decision must apply but where the offences in respect of which the detenu was accused are so interlinked and continuous in character and are of such nature that these affect continuous mainte nance of essential supplies and thereby jeo pardise the security of the State, then sub jection to other conditions being fulfilled, a man being in detention would not detract from the order being passed for preventive Detention. [825B C] 9. The decision in Rameshwar case is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the instant cases. [826C] 10. The contention that the period of parole from May 15, 1986 to February 28. 1987 could not he added to the maximum period of imprison ment of the Petitioner was not accepted. [827D] 11. The period of detention from May 14, 1986 till February 28 and 1987 to February 29, 1987 was not a period of limitation. The date of detention was not mentioned in the order dated February 27, 1986.

The petitioners were working as casual labourers in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. The petitioners were engaged as casual labour in the Telecom. The respondents, however, contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour, the wages paid to them are very low and far less than the salary and allowances paid to the regular employees of the Posts & Telegraphs department belonging to each of the categories referred to above and secondly no scheme has been prepared by the Union of India to absorb them regularly in its service and consequently they have been denied the benefits, such as increments, pension, leave facilities etc. which are enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly. The Union of india, however contended that the petitioners were not being regularly employed, they were not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employee were enjoying. The Court, HELD: 1. The scheme of absorption of casual labourers is a rational basis for absorbing as far as possible the casual labourers who have not completed 720 days of service over a period of three years or more. [602C] 2. The benefit of increased rates of daily wages will not be admissible to the casual semi skilled/skilled labour in whose case the continuous spells of duty are intervened by a period Of more than six months. [613D] 3. The benefits of increased rate of daily wage will not, however be admissible for the casual workers in whose cases the continuous spell of duty is intervened by an period of more than 6 months. These enhanced rates of wages will be without prejudice to absorption of the casual employees against regular vacancies as and when they occur. [502E] 4. The arrears of wages payable to the Casual labourers in accordance with this order shall be paid within four months from today. [625E] 5. The payment of arrears of salary payable to casual labourers shall be made within four weeks from today, failing which the petitioners shall be entitled to interest at the rate of 6% per annum from the date of this order.

The assessee, a resident of Bombay, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1950 51. The Income tax Officer, however, issued a notice under section 22(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, to the assessee, calling upon him to furnish a return of his income, and to submit a return showing an income below the taxable limit. The assessee filed a return on January 5, 1950, and the Income tax officer, after making a full assessment, issued notice under s.22(2), on January 6, 1950. The notice was served on the assessee on January 7, 1950 and the assessee filed his return on February 5, 1951, and on January 8, 1951. The assessment was completed on March 31, 1950 but the assessee did not file a return within the time fixed by the notice. The question for determination was whether the assessee was entitled to make a " voluntary return" under section 24(1) or section 24 (3) of that Act. Held, that the notice under the section was not a "public return" within the meaning of section 24 of the Act. The word "public" in section 24 means "a return of income, which is not chargeable to income Tax. The expression "public purpose" in the section means "to make a return". The expression 'public purpose ' in section 22 means "the purpose of making a return and the purpose of the return. The words "public purposes" in that section are not defined in the Act but are used in the sense of "public interest". The word 'public ' in the context of the section is not defined either in the Income Tax Act or in the Indian Penal Code. The object of the statute is to make the return a return which is in the nature of a return. It is not necessary that the return should be filed in the prescribed form. The purpose of section 22 is to enable the assessee to make his return and to file a revised return. If the return filed on January 4, 1950 was a return under section 23(1), the assessee could not be treated as a return filed under section 25(1). The expression public purpose ' is not used in section 23 (1) of Act. It means "public good". The words 'public purposes ' in that sub section are wide enough to include all kinds of public purposes. The legislature has used the expression "for the purpose" and the expression 'for the purposes of the Incometax Act is not restricted to the purposes for which the return is filed. The Legislature has used a word in the statute to mean "public". The legislature, therefore, has used it in the wider sense of the word " public purpose". The Legislature had used the word 'Public purpose ' and the word public purpose in the latter part of the definition is not confined to the purpose for which it is used. The use of the expression in the two parts of the sub section is wide enough. The language of the two sub sections is wide and the words "for any year" in sub section (1), are wide and include all types of public purpose. The first part of section 23 is wide, and it is not possible to say that even a return made in compliance with a notice issued under section 21(2). The second part of that section is wider than the one in section 25. The second portion of the said section is also wide enough and the third part of it is wide. The third part is wide in its amplitude and the fourth part is wider in its scope. The fourth part of sub section(1)(a) is wide as it is in its nature and is not limited to the objects for which a return is made. The last part of this section is in two parts.

The Central Government issued a notification dated 23.8.1982 under section 9 of the Act, declaring the election of the Directors of the respondent Bank to the Board of Directors of a corresponding new bank constituted under the Act. The said notification was challenged by the respondent bank in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that the Act contemplates both election and nomination of members of the Board and the choice between the two modes of appointment is left to the Central Government, and that the choice of the mode of appointment was left to be the appropriate mode of choosing the representatives of the employees, and, therefore, the choice was left open to the central Government, but it was not an unrestrained or unrestricted discretion, but a discretion which must be reasonably exercised so as to give effect to the true intent of the legislature as to the composition of the board of Directors. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The Act contemplates two modes for appointment of the representatives and the other, by nomination of one person out of the panel furnished by the representative Union of workmen or Association of non workmen, as the case may be, and if election were to be construed to be a proper mode of choice, the Central Govern ment would be justified in making the scheme in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India. [857C D] 1.2 The Act, therefore requires the Central Govt. to make the Scheme in consultation, with the Central Gov ernment, and the Central Gover nment to make a scheme in accordance with the provisions of the statute. [883D] 1:3 The Central Government is empowered to make an appropriate scheme for the constitution of the Boards of Directors so as not to include representatives of employees and other speci fied categories. The Central Governmen t is, therefore. competent to amend the Scheme to improve on the machinery for the conduct of an appropriate election, it is incumbent upon it, until any such amend ment is made, to work the present Scheme in such a way as to giving the maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives. [873E F] 1 :4 The Central Govt., is empowered under section 3(1) of the , to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions contained in the Act and the Scheme. The power to make such rules is subject to the provisions in the statute itself. The scheme is, however, subject to any rules made by the Central government under the statute and the scheme is subject only to the rules made under the Statute. [864G H] 1(a) The Central Gov tional Government is competent to make any scheme for constitution of a Board of directors so as t he Central Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, constitute the Board. The Act does not contemplate the appointment of a person as a member of the Central Board of the Company. The only provision in the Statute is that the Central or the State Government shall make a Scheme in accordance therewith. [854C D; 857A] 1.(b) The scheme, therefore cannot be said to be an unrestless or unrestricted power. [877E] 1 (c) The Act is not a law relating to the constitution or management of the company. It is a law which is intended to be implemented by the State. The State Government is not competent to alter the scheme. The Scheme is, in fact, a law made by Parliament.

The respondent was imposed penalties in the sum of Rs. 1,000/ on the respondent. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the penalty. The respondent preferred appeals to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal and made an interim prayer for stay of collection of the penalties. The Tribunal held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the recovery of the penalty imposed. The High Court held that it had the powers to stay proceedings as also the collection of penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Appellate Tribunal had no power to grant stay of recovery during the pendency of an appeal. HELD: The Appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power of stay as incidental or ancillary to the appellate jurisdiction, and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. [69 E] The Appellate Tribunals must be deemed to have been conferred with the power under the Code of Civil Procedure when trying a suit in respect of the matters specified in the section. [70 E] In the instant case, the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner and the Appellate Tribu nal were given the power by the Act to stay recovery of tax. The Act does not empower the Appellate Tribunals to stay any recovery proceedings or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue.

The respondent was a Sub Inspector of Police at the time of the departmental trial. He was charged under section 7 of the Police Act with having committed offences punishable under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The respondent was charged with having failed to discharge his duties and was convicted by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of dismissal was not in the first instance received by the Magistrate and forwarded to the police for inquiry. The enquiry ended in the dismissal of the respondent. The departmental inquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the Respondent in regard whereof the magisterial inquiry was held at an earlier stage. The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries did not affect the validity of the order of the dismissal. [682 B C] (ii) The departmental enquiry was only one step in regard to the misconduct and the departmental inquiry could not be said to be a mere step in the course of the trial. The order was not a mere administrative order but a mere executive order. The mere fact that the Superintendent of Police gave at first a good certificate to the respondent, in respect whereof the Magisterial inquiry had been held at the earlier stage, did not make any difference. [782 C D] (iii) The fact of the matter that in a subsequent event the police had received further complaint or that there was no magisterial enquiry in respect thereof would not affect its validity. [783 E] (iv) The mere circumstance that in some cases the police did not take any action against the respondent in regard thereto would not make the order invalid.

The appellant was appointed as a Specialists ' Grade II in the Central Government on February 8, 1971. He was promoted as a Director of Health Services on February 9, 1971 and was promoted to the post of Director of Medical Education on February 10, 1971, and was confirmed in the post on February 11, 1971 on the basis of the recommendations of the Third Pay Commission. The appellant was promoted on February 12, 1971 as Director of Public Health Services, Manipur. He challenged the promotion of the appellant on the ground that he was not qualified for promotion to supertime grade II on February 1, 1971 when he was promoted and that he should have been promoted from that date. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Appellant that the promotion to the supertime Grade II on Feb. 8,1971 was not a teaching hospital and, therefore, the appellant was fully qualified for being promoted to super time grade II. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The promotion of Dr. Sen and the post was not made in accordance with the relevant rule. [53G] 2. The post was converted into a specified post in supertime scale II and was sanctioned at Willingdon Hospital which is not a Teaching hospital and the appellant could not have been considered for promotion from the date on which Dr. P. Sen was promoted. [54H] 3. The question whether the appellant should be considered for the post which was deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971 on his invalidation of promotion of Mr. Sen would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [55A] 4. The fact that the appellant had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists ' grade and was senior to Dr. S. Sen, was not sufficient to entitle him to promotion. [56B] 5. The matter must remain at that stage and there is no justification for giving a direction that the Appellant should be consider for the posts which were deemed to be vacant in October 1971 on account of the invalidation of the promotion. The case must remain within the purview of the rule. If the appellant is not qualified, he would not have got the benefit of promotion from that year. [57C] 6. The order of promotion was not passed in accordance to the relevant rules. [58D] 7. The contention that the post in question was converted to a specified grade in super time scale II was not accepted by the High Court. [59F] 8. The appointment of Dr, Sen and Dr. D. Sen were made on February 13, 1971 in the same post and the promotion was made on March 11, 1972. The said post was subsequently converted into an additional post in the super time Scale II. The posts were converted into the specialists grade and the posts were filled in by promotion from those who were qualified to be promoted in the respective speciality in which the post is created. [60F] 9. The Government of India had issued a notification on February 14, 1971 whereby the Central Public Health Engineering Service was converted from a specified category to a particular post. The notification was issued on February 15, 1971 which was published in the Gazette on February 16, 1971 wherein it was stated that the posts in the specialities were converted to the specified posts in super Time Scale II and that the specialist ' grade posts were to be filled in, by promotion, from amongst those who had put in eight years of continuous service in that speciality. The respondent No. 1 was promoted in February 1971 and he was confirmed on February 21, 1971 with effect from February 11. 1971. The respondents Nos. 2 and 3 were promoted as Director in February, 1971 but the appellant did not join the post.

The appellants, who were the tenants of the land in dispute, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 (Act X of 1953) (for short, the Act). The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the land inherited by them and later transferred to his sons and wife were not hit by section 10A and section 19B of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts have rightly held that the lands inherited by the appellants and later transfer to their sons and husband were not covered by section 19 B. [632C] (2) The scheme of the Land Tenures (Amendment) Act, 1954, is to see that no one held in excess of the permissible area and since by the gift to the son or wife the latter had only lands within permissible limits, there was no frustration of the policy of the law. [732D] (3) The object of the legislation is to provide for the acquisition of surplus area for the resettlement of tenants ejected, or to be ejected, under clause (a) of section 10 A. [832E] (4) The legislature has not intended to give any time to the heir to ascertain the assets he has inherited, make the choice of his 'reserved area ' which he likes to keep and make the necessary declaration. [758F] (5) The purpose of the enactment is to give some time to a heir to determine the assets, he has acquired, make a declaration of his lands within a prescribed time. The legislature intended that the surplus pool will be adversely affected if gifts and other transfers which will skim off surplus were to be allowed.

The plaintiffs claimed the Zamindari of Amarshah as an impartible estate, devolving by the rule of primogeniture, and the other estate of Amarashah.
