The defendants contended that the genealogical table set up by the plaintiffs was incorrect, that by the order of the Governor of Madhya Pradesh dated November 9, 1951, the Zamindari was conferred upon the 1st defendant Dayaram as he was found suitable to hold the Zamindari and the decision of the Compensation Officer regarding Malguzari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951 had become binding and conclusive against the plaintiffs because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two months from the date thereof and the plaintiffs were on that account not entitled to claim the compensation paid or payable in respect of the Malgu zari lands. The trial court held that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that the lands in dispute were impartible and that the decision was binding on the plaintiffs. The High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the defendants were in possession of the lands and that they were entitled to the compensation. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of Governor recognising Dayaram to be the successor on the death of Amshah was not binding and the order was contrary to the customs and the law governing the Zamindari. [319 C] (ii) The decision of a Governor in 1950 declaring Dayaram to he the successor of the common ancestor of the plaintiffs as an estate was not conclusive and could not be reopened in a suit filed more than six years after that date. [340 D] (iii) The High Courts were in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awardable to the plaintiffs, because no appeal or revision was filed by the defendants against the decision. [341 E] (iv) The question regarding the pro prietary rights may in ordinary course be raised only in a claim against the State, and if that claim be decided against the claim ' ant in a summary inquiry held by the Compensation officer, a suit to set aside the decision must be filed within two month from that date and if no suit is filed, the order becomes final and conclusive.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that the tenant had committed default in payment of rent. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court took the view that the provisions contained in section 12(3) (a) of the Act do not apply to the suit, but that the suit was governed by the provisions of section 12 (3) of Act. The Bombay High Court held that the dispute as to standard rent was to be raised within one month from the service of the notice on the tenant. The appellant landlord appealed to this Court. HELD: The Bombay view is that the question whether the provisions in section 13(3)(a) are applicable to the case is not limited only to a dispute raised within a month of the service or the notice terminating the tenancy by raising a dispute as contemplated in section12(3). [632 D] The Bombay decision in Ambalal 's case (supra) and in Chunilal Shivlal vs Chimanlal Nagindas took the contrary view and held that in order to attract the applicability of section 13 (3)(b) of Bombay Act, the dispute in regard to standard rents must be raised at the latest before the expiry of one month. [633 E] The Gujarat High Court in Amalal ' 's Case (supra), held that section 12 of the Bombay Act does not apply. [643 D] In the instant case, the Bombay High court took the same view and dismissed the appeal.

The respondent company was a director of the respondent company. The respondent company appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the company. In the course of the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1939 to 1943, the Income tax Officer held that the directors of a company had a controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 2 (21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, read with section 66(1) of that Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was no room for doubt that the respondent Company had a control interest in the respondent 's company as contemplated under section 2(21) and that the Directors of the appellant company had no controlling interest therein. The Tribunal, however, held that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the directors had a "a controlling interest" in the company as envisaged by section2 (21). The High Court, on reference, answered in the affirmative. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the shares held by the respondent were not "a control interest" within the meaning of section 2 of the Act. It was not necessary that in order to have "a Controlling interest" the person or persons who hold the majority of the shares must have a beneficial interest in them, and as between them and their beneficiaries the beneficial interest is vested in them. The controlling interest remains vested in the Aluminium Ltd. and is at no time vested in Mr. L. G. L., G. Bash. The directors of an Indian company may well be regarded as having "a governing interest" and the right to vote is vested with them, though as between themselves and their beneficiary the beneficial interests are vested in him, though in the eye of the law, the controlling interest remained vested in it, though, as between the shareholders and their trustees, the beneficial ownership is vested by the latter. The control of the Aluminium company is vested only in the shareholders, and the rights to vote are vested with the shareholders. The shares held in the appellant 's name are not "an interest" but "a controlled interest" which is vested on the shareholders in the latter, and, therefore, the shares cannot be said to have a controlling interests in the shares. The words "a managing interest" are used in the context of the definition of "a person" in section 2, and it is not necessary to refer to the definition in section 3 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as it is only a person who holds the majority or shares of the shareholders of the Company. The word "a " controlling interest " in section 4 of the Income Tax Act means "a right to hold the shares as trustees and may even be accountable to their beneficiaries and may be brought to book for exercising their votes in breach of trust, nevertheless, as from the date of the application of the provisions of the section, the managing interest remains vest in the assessee. The expression "a" in that section means "any interest in a company when such a person acquires, by purchase or otherwise, the majority shares of a shareholder". The word 'a ' in section 5 of the Companies Act means a person holding the majority and not a person in whom the majority is held. The definition of the word "person" in s.2(21), therefore, includes a person whose interest is acquired by purchase, or otherwise. The term "a company" in this section means a company which has a controlling share in a Company when such person acquires by purchase and otherwise, any share in the share held by him. The company is a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and is a body corporate. The managing interest of the assessee company is not a controlled company. It is a controlled Company.

The respondent was appointed as Accounts Superintendent in the appellant Board. He was promoted as Accounts Assistant on 30th December, 1966. On 30th November, 1966, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. Examination. On 1st October, 1957, some of the persons junior ted to the Respondent were promoted as an Accounts Assistant. On 31st December, 1967, some others junior to him were promoted. On 2nd October, 1967 some persons senior to the appellant were promoted to the post of Accounts Assistant and the respondent was promoted to that post with effect from that date. On 3rd October, 1968, some other persons junior in the respondent 's service were promoted and the appellant was promoted on the basis of seniority cum merit. On 4th October, 1969, some officers junior to them were promoted, but the respondent did not pass the examination. On 5th January, 1970, some employees junior to her were promoted but the appellant did not passed the examination and therefore, the respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the promotion of the respondent. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent is exempted from passing the Departmental Examination and the Resolution of the Board dated 5th Jan. 1970, was not applicable to the allottees. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court was in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions and holding that there was no longer open to the respon dent to rely on the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Resolution of 5th February, 1970 is not intended to cover the case of allottees and merely because the allottees were excluded from the operation of the Resolution, the inference that the allottees are exempt from passing 'of the examination is not justified. [515C D] 2. The resolution of the board dated 5.1.1970, which was passed by the Board in pursuance of certain proceedings of the Government referred to in the Resolution itself, is not meant to cover cases of allottees. The Board itself considered the ques tion in all its aspects and resolved that passing of the examination was not insisted in future also, and if passing of S.S., Examination was not insisting prior to that Resolution in the case o f allotees for promotion to the cadre of Accounts Superintendents, the conclusion of the High Courts cannot be upheld as the binding nature of the regulations passed by Board under section 79(c) has not been taken due note of. [511D E] 3. The Regulations framed by the board under section 80(c), have not been challenged in the present case as the Regulations framed under section79(c). The Resolution was not intended for cover the cases of allotees and merely Because the allottees had been excluded from passing of ' the examination, the presumption that the allotment was exempt from the passing of a ' examination is no justified. Further before the Resolution there is nothing to indicate that the allottee were not required to pass the examina tion. The conclusion of High Court cannot be sustained as the decision of the Single Judge of the Karnataka High Court is not correct. [615E F] 4. The decision of this Court in the State of Mysore vs M. P. Rajappa, [1968] 1 S.C.R. 869, relied on.

The petitioner 's son Suman Behera was taken from his home in police custody at about 8 a.m. on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police of Jaraikela Police Outpost under Police Station Bisra, Distt. The petitioner ' s son Suman was taken to the police custody in police remand. The police arrested the petitioner and his mother in police detention. The mother of the petitioner was taken into custody on 1st December, 1987 by respondent no.6. The father of the Petitioner 's daughter was taken in police lock up at about 9 a. m. on the same day. The Petitioner ' s daughter was also taken into police custody. The husband of the deceased was taken away by respondent Nos. 6 and 7. The wife of the victim was taken back to her home in the police remand home. The brother of the husband of respondent No,6 was taken by respondent nos. 6 & 7 to the Police Station. The Police Inspector of Jarikela Police Station, who was on duty at the relevant time, was informed by respondent NO.6 that the petitioner ' son Suman had been taken away from his house in police confinement. The deceased was also informed that the husband and wife of respondent Nos 6 and7 were taken away. The daughter of the brother of respondent no,6 died on 1 12.1987. The respondent No.,6 filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for determining the claim of compensation for contravention of fundamental right to life guaranteed under Article 21 of the constitution. The petition was contested by the petitioner on the ground that the claim was not maintainable as the petitioner had not been impleaded as a party to the petition. The Additional Solicitor General, however, did not dispute the liability of the State for payment of compensation in this proceeding for violation of fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 21 and 22 of the Consti tution of India. The State contended that the petition was not competent as the petition had been filed by the mother of Suman Behra, who had been impleaded in the petition, and that the mother had been given the benefit of monetary compensation in proceedings under Article 226 of the Constitu tion. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the case put up by the police of the alleged escape of Suman was not acceptable. The Court, however held that the State had failed to establish that the death of Suman had resulted from the commission of the offence and that there was no violation of the fundamental right guaranteed under article 21 of Constitution. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right, imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental rights of the citizen. [608C] 1.2 The Court has not only the power and jurisdiction but also an obligation to grant relief in exercise of its jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226 of t he Constitution to the victim or the heir of the victims whose fundamental rights under Article 19 of the Con stitution are established to have been flagrantly infringed by calling upon the State to repair the damage done by its officers. [613D] 1:3. The compensation is in the nature of compensa tion for contravention and enforcement of fundamental Rights guaranteed by the Constitution. [508C D] 1 :4.

The petitioner, a prisoner, was sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by him to the President of India for commutation of the sentence were rejected by the President. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the President rejecting his petitions. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, which includes the freedom of the Press, is not an absolute right, nor indeed does it confer any right on the Press to have an unrestricted access to means of information. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right of the press to have a unrestricted access through the medium of an interview of the two prisoners who are sentenced to life. [1187G] 2. The constitutional right of freedom of expression conferred under article 19 (1)(b) of Constitution, is neither an absolute nor absolute right nor indeed did it confer an absolute or absolute right on any citizen to have such an unrestricted right. [1108C] 3. The fundamental right to free speech and freedom of press is not absolute right but is not a absolute right. It is not merely a right to be informed about the right, but also a right of free speech. [1087G H] 4. The freedom of Press is not one of the rights conferred by Article 19(2) of our Constitution. The Constitution is not intended to confer any fundamental right on a citizen to carry on any trade or business. [1008C D] 5. The expression "public order" in article 19 is not defined in the Constitution. It does not mean that the press is entitled to exercise its freedom of freedom. The press is free to have access to the means of communication. [1018D] 6. The petitioners have been asking for permission to interview the prisoners, the newspapers, the Times of India, India Today, the Press Trust of India and the United News of India to interview them. The representatives of the Times, the newspaper, India today, the press Trust of Indian India and United News, India, are not expressly referred to in clause (4) but that does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press. [102D E] 7. The provisions of the Jail Manual for the Superintendence and Management of Jails, which is applicable to Delhi, provide that every prisoner under a sentence of death shall be allowed such interviews and other communications with his relatives, friends, legal advisers and approved religious ministers. But it does not provide that no newspapermen will be allowed. [103E F] 8. The existence of a free Press does not indicate or spellout any legal obligations on the citizen to supply the information to him. The fact that the prisoners are willing to be interviewed, does not necessarily mean that they can always and without good reasons be denied the opportunity to interview a condemned prisoner. [104F] 9. The question whether a newspapermen who can broadly, and without great fear of contradiction, be termed as friends of the society be denied an opportunity to interviews a condemned person, is a matter for the Court to decide. If such an application is made to the Superintendent of Jail, he will be free to consider the same on merits and in accordance with the jail regulations. [105G H; 106A] 10. The Court cannot ignore that the petitioner has been asking the permission to interviews the prisoners. The petition is dismissed.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd. on January 19, 1950. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956, but the respondent 's application for damages to the extent of Rs. 22, 1956 was dismissed for default by the Judicial Commissioner. The respondent filed an appeal to the High Court which dismissed the appeal. The High Court held that the surety bond was executed in and for the purposes of the particular proceedings which were pending before the District Judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge. The appeal to this Court was filed by the appellant on the ground that the Subordinate judge who tried the suit was incompetent to enforce the surety bonds executed by the respondent as he was neither the successor nor the successor in office nor the assign of the District judge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The surety bond is a part of the proceedings pending before a District Judge. It is impossible to accept the contention that the Receiver owed no duty or obligation in respect of the tea garden. He was put in possession of the Tea garden in his capacity as a Receiver and indeed parties had made contentions from time to time as to whether the tea gardens were managed by the Receiver economically and efficiently. The surety bonds would therefore cover the loss occasioned to the tea plantation due to the Receiver 's negligence in the performance of his duties. [360 E F] (2) The bond is executed both by the receiver and the appellant in favour of "Sri Ramani Mohan Goswami the District Court". The surety Bond is a whole of the proceeding pending before it and on transfer of it to the Subordinate Court. The bond would therefore be enforceable at the instance of the presiding officer of the court. [361 E F; 362 A] (3) The appellant was put into possession of tea garden in the capacity as Receiver and was put to the custody of the Receiver. The sureties bond was a part and parcel of the Proceedings pending before him. The bail bond was not executed by him as he had not been either the successor or the assignor of the district judge. [362 B] (4) The High court was right in holding that the appellant was liable to make good the loss caused to the Tea Garden by the fire.

The appellant, a dealer in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller, various quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. Wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants, rejecting the contention raised by the appellant that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller. The Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales Tax held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no "sale" within the meaning of the Act. The High Court held that there was a contract between the appellant and the State pursuant to which the goods were sold within the definition of the word 'sale ' in section 2(h) of the Uttar Pradesh (Sale of Goods) Act, 1959 and that the sales made to the State Government were not taxable. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Courts were right in holding that the transactions of supply did not result in sales and were on that account not exposed to sales tax. [534 C] (2) The expression "sale " in section 3(h), means the money consideration for sale of goods, and the expression "purchase" in section 4(1) means the price paid or payable for the goods. The expression 'purchase ' in the section means the amount paid or promised to be paid or agreed to be made by the dealer to the purchaser. The word 'purchase " in the context of the definition in section 5(1), means a transfer of property in the goods for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration. The words "purchase " and "purchase of goods" in the definition are not defined in the Act but in the U .P. Sales tax Act. [511 D E] (3) The word "purchase ' is not defined either in the Sales Tax Acts or in the Indian Sale Tax Acts. The definition of "sale ' is wide enough to include a transfer by way of sale of property. The term "purchase", in the sense of a sale, means a sale of the goods by one person to another. The sale of a property in a goods is not a sale. The purchase of goods is a transfer for cash, deferred payment, or other consideration. [634 E F] (4) The definition in the Sale Tax Act is wide and comprehensive enough to cover all transactions of sale. [613 A] (5) The words 'purchase of property ' in s.2(h)(i) and (j) of section 3 of the , are wide enough and include a sale by way or by way, of a contract of sale, but the expression 'sale of goods ' in that section is wide. The legislature has used the expression in the Explanation to the section. The Explanation to section 3 is wide in its amplitude and covers all transactions which are not covered by the definition.

The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was acquitted on May 26, 1986. The State Government issued a detention order on August 7, 1986 under section 3(1) of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The appellant challenged the order of detention on the ground that the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the question as to whether there was sufficient cause for the detention of the appellant. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the report of the Advisory Board was more than three weeks after the detention which commenced on the making of the order, though it was within three months from the date of the second order of Detention. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The report of such an Advisory Board is not a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the Constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date on which its report or beyond the period of three months after the date o f detention. [206E] 2. The question to which the Advisory Boards have to apply its mind is whether on the date when the detention order was made, there was no sufficient cause justifying the detention. If the report is not made within three weeks, it is no answer to saying that the reference, though not made in three weeks was made before the hearing of the case. If a reference to an Advisory board is to be made within 3 weeks, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it is within three month from the day of the first order of the detention, and therefore, the detaining authori ty must be held to have applied its minds to the questions as to what the Advisory board has to apply their mind. [207E F] 3. The Court was not confronted with the present situation at all. The fact that the Advisory Committee has to consider the question whether there is sufficient cause or not for the order made, does not mean that the Court is not confronted to say whether the report though not obtained within three days, was obtained before the hear ing of the matter. If it is not so, the Court would not be entitled to extend the jurisdiction of the Board to the consideration of the question. [208G H] 4. The order of preventive detention should have been made, knowing full well that there was in its opinion sufficient cause. If there were no fresh facts, the maximum period for which a person may be detained shall not extend beyond the expiry of the period for making a subsequent detention order. [209A B] 5. The detaining authority has to satisfy itself that there is in its mind sufficient cause to justify the detention and that there are no sufficient grounds for the same. If, however, the report does not disclose that the detenu was not aware of the fact that he was not informed of the facts, it would be open to the detaining Authority to make a fresh order of his detention. The detenu is entitled to be released forthwith.

The respondent, a father of the respondent, filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement dated 18th January, 1977. The respondent filed an application for setting aside the award on the ground that the award was not remitted under section 16(5) of the Act. The trial court rejected the objections filed beyond the period of limitation and for the reasons that (1) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the award, (2) the time for making an application to set aside the same had expired and no such application was made (3) the award had not been remitted under Section 16(4) of Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent had not given the notice to the respondent about the pendency of the arbitration proceedings; (ii) the period for making the application to setting aside an award had expired; and (iii) the judgment of the trial court in Special Civil Suit No. 14 of 1978 was not set aside under section 30 and (4) that the arbitrator had not signed the award. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The High Court was right in dismissing the application in the manner it did. [537C] 2. The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute to the arbitration of the named arbitrator. [540D] 3. The fact that the respondent was dead at the time the suit had been instituted or decree was passed or some such other ground which could have the effect of rendering the court entirely lacking in jurisdiction in respect of the subject matter of the suit or over the parties to it. [541E] 4. The judgment of this Court in Seth Hira Lal Patni vs Shri Kali Nath, ; , relied on.

The appellant, a mortgagee of a mortgage debt, was the mortgagor of a suit for recovery of a loan advanced before or after the commencement of the Act. The respondent, who was the mortgagee of the mortgage debt and the appellant, was a sub mortgagee, filed a suit against the appellant for recovery on the ground that the mortgage was not an absolute interest and that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the proviso to sub section (1) of section 36 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The proviso to section 36(1) makes it quite clear that in exercise of the powers conferred on the Court or to be exercised either in any suit to which this Act applies or in any other suit brought by a borrower for relief under the section and (ii) that the Court is called upon to exercise all or any of the power conferred on it by the section if the Court has reason to believe that the exercise of one or more of the said powers will give relief to the borrower. [118 E F] (ii)(a) The words and that he had not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of sub section(1), are wide enough to include a proceeding in execution for any of those purposes mentioned in clauses (a), (b) or (c) of Section 2(22) of the Income tax. [119 F] The words "all the rights of the mortgagee" used by their Lordships in the passage quoted above, and it was not necessary to refer to them in the present case. [120 G] (b)(i) In the present ease, the respondent 's decree must be taken to have been passed "in a suit to Which this Act applied" and the respondent had not obtained the notice of the suit. [121 E] (c)(ii) The expression "all rights of a mortgagee" in section 2(23) of Income tax is wide enough, and the words "any suit or proceeding instituted or filed on or after that date and includes a proceeding for execution for the recovery of the loan advanced after the date of the commencement.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The properties were divided into two parts, one by the father and the other by the son. The appellant was a coparcener of the joint family. The respondents contended that the transfers were made by Venkatacharyulu in favour of the appellant in view of past illicit cohabitation with her, such past cohabitation was the motive and not the consideration for the transfers. The High Court held that the transfer was made by the appellant to the appellant by way of gifts and not in consideration of the past cohabitations. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The transfers were without consideration and were by way Of gifts. The gifts were not hit by section 6(h) of the , by reason of the fact that they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubine for her past services. [45 D] (ii) The transfer was without consideration, and was invalid. The transfers under Exs. A 1 and A 2 were not invalid. [46 E] (iii) The gifts are not hit either by section 4(h), or section 6 of the . [46 G] (iv) The properties gifted under exhibit A 1 were not liable to be treated under section 2(d) of Act. [47 C] (v) The gift was not hit under section 6 (h) because the gifts were made in consideration for past cohabiting. The gift is not hit on section 6.

The respondent, a company, was incorporated in the year 1948. The company was incorporated on 5.12.75. The respondent, who was the assignee of the policies, was granted a certificate of registration under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Income Tax Officer, however, issued a notice under section 227(3)(vi) of that Act to the respondent, for payment of interest for the period after the date of maturity of the insur ance policy. The appellant, who had been granted a Certificate of Registration under section 225(3), filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice issued by the Income tax Officer. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the delay in making the requisite statement under section226(3 ) of the Act, by the L.I.C. was not due to the appellant inasmuch as it was payable only to the assignee, Smt. Kamalabai G. Ranade, and not the defaulter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The delay in filing the requisite statements under section227(3 )(vi), of the income Tax Act 1961, was the result of misconstruction of the provision and misappreciation of its liability thereunder. Performance of this statutory obligation by the appellant, in the present case, being after inordinate delay, award of interest to the assignor of the policy to whom the payment thereunder had to be made even according to the stand of the LI. C. [114B C] 2. The inordinate delay in the making of the requisite declaration under section 22(3A) of Income Tax, 1961, by L. I.C., in the instant case, was not attributable to the assessee inasmuch as the Ll.C itself had taken the stand throughout that the moneys due under the policies were held by it for and on behalf Of the assignee and not by the defaulter, and, therefore, the making thereof was not a valid ground for refusing to entertain the claim of the respondent. [115E F] 3. The question of revoca tion of the notices under section 228(3). of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1976, by which the amount of the matured policies within the time given by the I.T.O. was reduced to Rs. 1,00,000/ was not raised in the writ peti tion. The contention that such a statement was not made since it involved the likelihood of exposing the L I.I.,C. or any of its officers to personal liability has, therefore no merit. [116F G] 4. The mere fact that the L1.C had made the requisite Statement on oath under section 223(3); did not make the requisite averment in the notice under Section 226(2) of Act, as envisaged in clause (vi) thereof, instead of in doing so. [117G] 5. The unexplained delay in giving the requisite information under section 173(3 A) of 1961 Act, in this case, is, therefore clearly justified.

The appellant was the Chief Justice of the Madhya Pradesh High Court. He was appointed as the Chief Judge of the High Court on August 1, 1963. He filed a suit against the Chief justice and the Chief Justices of the said High Court for a declaration that the order of the Chief judge dated August 1. 1963 was illegal and void. The suit was decreed by the trial court on March 31, 1963 and the appeal was dismissed on March 30, 1963, but the High court dismissed the appeal on March 29, 1963 on the ground that the appeal had been filed within time. The appellant then filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Courts for a writ of certiorari quashing the order dated March 31. 1963 and for a direction to the Chief Judges to dispose of the appeal within a specified time. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High 'Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition and that the application was barred by limitation. Held, that the question whether a suit, appeal or application under a particular local law is of a kind similar to one for which a period of limitation is prescribed in the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, is a question of fact and not a question which can be decided by the High courts in exercise of their jurisdiction under article 227 of the Consti tution. The first limb of sub section (2) of section 29 is concerned only with proceedings of this kind, that is, proceedings under special or local law for which the period of Limitation is prescribed. The second limb of section 30 is concerned with proceedings under a special or general law for the same type of appeal, and that is to say, proceedings in special or special law for such an appeal. The third limb of the sub section is concerned merely with proceedings in a special and local law, for which no period of time is prescribed by the first schedule. The words "where any special or other local law prescribes for any suit, Appeal or application a period different from the period prescribed therefor by the First schedule" occurring in the first limb are not intended to be used in the sense of a special law. The word "where" in the second limb is used in a sense of the term "where". The first part of sub s.(2) is concerned, only with the proceedings of the special orlocal law forwhich a period is prescribed, and for the purpose of determining any period of limitations prescribed for any such suit, appeals or application by any special and other local laws. The fourth limb of subsection (2), is concerned not with proceedings for the recovery of any amount due under the decree or order of a court, but with proceedings relating to the recovery thereof. The last limb of subs.(2), therefore, is concerned in the instant case only with proceeding of the suit, and not with the execution of the decree. The High Court was right in holding that the suit was barred under article 156 of the First Sch. to the Code of Civil Procedure.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, was directed to stop their buses at the bus stand fixed by the District Magistrate. The appellant challenged the validity of the order before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the District Magis trate had no power to appoint any area as a bus stand under section 76 of the Act, and that the order made under section 77 of the , was unassailable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The District Magistra trate has been authorised by the State Government under section 68(2)(r) of the . The Regional Transport Authority had no jurisdiction to fix the places for the bus stands. The power to issue a notification fixing a bus stands was implied in section 68 (2)(t) of Act. [766C D] 2. The Regional transport Authority had been authorised under section 78 of the Motor Vehicles Act to pass an order fixing the places of the bus Stand. The order made by the Regional Transport Authori ties was open to revision under section 64 A by the state Transport Authority. Such a power should be given specifically by the statute and that, the power to compel persons in charge of motor buses to stop only at certain places for their pur pose of taking up or setting down passengers was a matter which relating to motor traffic and that there was a specifi cial provision in section68(2) (r) for that pur pose. [779E F] 3. The State Transport Authority could not exercise the power of fixing a Bus stand under Section 76 of Act and that could be done only under section 69(2). [767F] 4. The provisions relating to parking places and halting places have no application to a permanent bus stand which was a sort of radiating centre of all the bus traffic in the town. The Municipal Council had been empowered by the Government under Section 68(1) of . The power under section 70(2), therefore, could be exercised only by the Divisional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the district Magistrate. [780F] 5. The word 'control ' in section 76(2 ) of the is wide enough to include the power under Section 70(1). The power of the State Transport authority to issue the notification fixing the place of the Bus stand is implied in Section 68 (1) and that power to direct persons in Charge of motor vehicles to stop at certain place for the pur pose cannot be equated with the Regional Trans port Authority constituted under the Act. The words 'control of transport vehicles ' in Section 76(1), therefore are wide enough. [781C D, F] 6. The expression 'control" in section 77(2 )(r), therefore is wide and comprehensive enough to cover the power conferred on the State Govern ment under section 73 of the act. [783F] 7. The Act does not confer any power on the Regional transport authority to fix a bus Stand under section 75 of the for the purpose of the said chapter. The powers under section 74 of the are confined to the question of determination of parking places, halting places and landing places. The exercise of the power is confined to a question of determining the parking places or halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the regional Transport Authority as held by this Court in T.B. It is open to the Regional Authority to take action immediately for determining any convenient place or places within the Town Area of Baldev (Mathura) as a Bus Stand.

The appellants were convicted under section 7 of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. The trial court convicted all the accused persons but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction of the appellants. The High Court set aside their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellants were guilty of an attempt to commit the offence of export. HELD: (i) The sufficiency of the actus reus is a question of law which had led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission of a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt for committing it. [682 C] (ii) The mere fact that the accused was not present at the time when the offence was committed would not make the offence an offence. [667 D] (iii) The fact that a person may be convicted of an attempted attempt to export or abet the export of paddy does not make him an offence under section 3(a) of the Act. [666 E] (iv) The absence of an intention to commit an offence is not a mere preparation on the part of the accused. [665 G] (v) The question whether a person is guilty of attempt to committing an offence or not is a matter of law. The sufficiency or the sufficiency of an actus is one of fact which has led to difficulties because of necessity of distinguish between acts, which are mere preparatory to commission of the crime, but those which were sufficiently proximate and to it could be said to amount an attempt on the person committing the offence. The adequacy of the actsus reis is a mixed question of fact and law.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business as managing agents of the respondent company. The respondent company was incorporated under a deed of partnership dated November 1, 1948, and the appellant was the Managing Agent of the company. In the assessment year 1949 50 the Income tax Officer included the income of the appellant as income from the business of the Company. The Income tax Appellate Tribunal held that the appellant had not earned any part of the Managing Agency commission which had been paid by the company to the transferees and were not liable to tax in respect of the same. The Tribunal, however, held that as the appellant did not earned a part of its Managing Agency, the remuneration for the Managing agency was not liable for tax in the assessment years 1949 50 and 1949 51. The High Court, on reference, held in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The managing agency agreement in the present case was an indivisible contract for a whole year 's remuneration on the completion of a whole period of the work. The agreement was an independent contract for the whole year and was not a mere agreement of transfer of the managing agency. The terms of the agreement showed that the assignor and the assignee were to be treated as one entity and that on assignment the assignee became the Managing agent as if his name had been inserted in the Managing Agents Agreement from the beginning, and that the continuity of the said Managing Agency was preserved thereby and that whoever satisfies the description of the Directors of the transferor and the transferee, either as part of their deed of transfer or independent thereof. [371 E F] (ii) The agreement in question was an integral part of a contract for remuneration on completion of the whole period. The managing agent was to be responsible only to the assignee for the payment of the entire year ' s remuneration. The remuneration for that year was not by itself enough to vest in the assignee a beneficial right to the remuneration of the year, such a right may arise by virtue of a specific or implied term as between the transferor & the transferee either as parts of the deed of assignment or independent thereto. [372 E F; 373 A B] (iii) The Managing Agency Agreement in the instant case was not an indivisible agreement for remuneration but was a composite contract for one year ' and the remuneration to be income by way of profits or gains from the Business. The appellant was not entitled to the amount by way Of remuneration not as per the agreement. [373 E] (iv) The appellant had been given the right to receive the entire remuneration did not depend on any specific term between the assignors and the assignee, but on the fact that what was transferred was an income bearing asset which carried with it a right to its entire income that fell due after the date of assignment.
